title: Does the Mixer Matter ? Paired-Seed Ablations of Tiny Bilingual Language Models
abstract: We report paired-seed architecture ablations from the development of Sophea Artemis, our in-house Greek-English model family. Every arm trains on the same 3B targets with a shared tokenizer and recipe; models range from 54M to 759M total parameters and roughly 54M to 124M active parameters. The main finding is that, at this tiny scale, stored capacity matters far more than mixer design. On a fixed held-out test, replacing the dense feed-forward blocks of a recurrent/attention hybrid with sixteen routed experts, at nearly the same approximate active parameters, lowers loss by 0.079 (Greek) and 0.112 (English) nats per target, and doubling to 32 experts lowers it by a further 0.022 and 0.031, at every paired seed. Reusing a four-layer block three times recovers about 40-44% of the gap between a shallow and an independently deep model, consistent with looped-Transformer results. In contrast, the choice among grouped-query attention (GQA), Gated DeltaNet (GDN) hybrids and a Kimi Delta Attention (KDA) hybrid moves loss by only about 0.01-0.02 nats; a 1:1 GDN/GQA hybrid is the one dense variant that improves on GQA in both languages at every held-out seed. In bits per character, Greek and English held-out losses are similar despite a 74.49%/25.51% training split, and synthetic mathematics, which comes from a collection outside the training sources, is the hardest Greek test component and gains least from added experts. Cached decoding needs its own qualification: trained models passed cached-versus-full logit checks only under a fixed-reduction inference policy, which itself changes 1.4-2.8% of next-token argmax choices relative to native evaluation. All results are conditional on one recipe and scale.

title: Large Language Models in Crowd Management Systems: A Critical Review of Cognitive Intelligence, Applications, and Challenges — Reproducibility Package
abstract: Reproducibility materials accompanying the critical evidence-map review of large language models in crowd management systems. The archive preserves 317 candidate entries, 275 unique candidates, 79 mapped records (38 core and 41 adjacent/supporting), 19 contextual references, and 177 non-retained records. Relevant full-text sections were inspected for 36 of 38 core studies. Of 54 evaluated or simulation records, 30 report explicit comparators and 14 have numerically extracted outcomes. Independent human screening of a random sample of 55 records gave 47/55 three-category agreement (Cohen’s kappa 0.7642). Version 1.1.0 adds a function-by-design evidence map of the 38 core records and an extraction-based nine-item CCIF reporting checklist for 23 direct component and crowd-related task studies (207 criterion-level indications, with locators and reproducible descriptive summaries). The checklist is not an independently validated quality instrument. Original screening decisions and extraction records remain unchanged. Literature cutoff: 22 November 2026. The archive provides exact queries, evidence and access ledgers, anonymized paired decisions, author-approved reconciliation, codebook, six figures and reproducibility scripts. No personal reviewer details, third-party articles, original datasets, live operational records, model implementations or physical control instructions are redistributed.

title: HoloSplat: Real-Time Token Streaming for Feed-Forward Human Reconstruction
abstract: Live free-viewpoint video streaming of humans enables immersive telepresence and interactive XR applications. However, this requires reconstructing each frame in real time, transmitting the data within strict bandwidth budgets, and decoding it on lightweight client GPUs. Existing approaches, whether relying on per-frame optimization or feed-forward inference, generate massive 3D Gaussian payloads that exceed practical streaming limits, while aggressive compression severely degrades rendering quality. In this work, we present HoloSplat, a real-time streaming framework for human-centric volumetric video. HoloSplat splits a feed-forward reconstructor before its Gaussian head, introducing a multi-rate streaming codec driven by server-side token compression and client-side token restoration. On the server side, we apply opacity-guided token pruning, PCA-based dimensionality reduction, and lossless geometry coding for token anchors. On the client side, a feature reconstruction hypernetwork is fused into the Gaussian head to recover compression-induced quality loss. Furthermore, we introduce Neural Session Calibration (NSC), which rapidly fine-tunes the Gaussian head online using incoming camera views during a warm-up phase. This resolves quality degradation from novel camera parameters and varying capture conditions with zero per-frame overhead. In our evaluations, HoloSplat averages 32.2 FPS on four RTX 5090 GPUs at 50 Mbit/s. It decodes each frame into 3D Gaussians in 22.1 ms on an RTX 3050 Ti laptop GPU, transmitting 22.8$\times$ less data than uncompressed float32 Gaussians, while calibrated decoding improves PSNR by 1.050 dB.

title: Learning Multimodal Representations from Partially Paired, Small-Scale Data
abstract: Modeling multimodal data from partially paired samples is critical for advancing domains like biomedicine, where vast unimodal datasets and foundation models exist but paired data remains scarce. Existing fusion methods rely on large-scale paired datasets, limiting their use in scenarios with incomplete pairing. We introduce CAMEO, an adversarial learning-based modality fusion framework that integrates modalities from small, partially paired datasets. Combining any pre-trained unimodal encoder with a cross-modal latent alignment mechanism, CAMEO learns shared representations requiring only minimal paired samples. Evaluated on computational pathology tasks such as niche classification and cell type composition prediction, CAMEO achieves superior data efficiency, outperforming contrastive approaches like CLIP in low paired-data regimes, and highlighting the benefits of adversarial alignment when paired annotations are scarce. To facilitate further research, we additionally release a fully annotated HuggingFace dataset comprising three organs and paired image and gene expression modalities. By extending fusion methods to address limited pairing and small-scale datasets, we provide a framework that advances multimodal learning and broadens its applicability to real-world biomedical problems.

title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

title: Deneb-Vritra: Descriptions, Edges and Names Examined by Blocking Via Restoring Token Representations and Attention
abstract: Laya is a 421M-parameter encoder that answers a question about a text in one pass: each answer option, written as a name plus a description, gets a marker token, and one score is read from the network at each marker. We first confirm that such models can follow an option's name when it contradicts the description; the question is where in the network this happens. We locate it. On 951 synthetic questions we move each name onto another option's description and count how often the model picks the option with the right name (the name shortcut): 53% for the released checkpoint, 59% for our fine-tune v1, 11% for a fine-tune with name randomisation. On a 320-item sample, blocking attention from each marker to its own name tokens in layers 14 to 17 of 28 cuts v1's shortcut from 67% to 16% (19% on two schemas held out from component selection) while accuracy with the original names stays at 90%; blocking marker edges to the question, other options or text has no effect. No single head matters (largest effect 9 points), and restoring clean marker states undoes the swap from layer 16. Attention mass tracks the window by layer but not by head. Repeated on 5 checkpoints (released, fine-tuned, name-randomised, and a pair trained without two schemas), the knockout finds similar layers; in the name-randomised ones, blocking the description edges instead brings the shortcut back to 56-58%, so the read persists and is outvoted. Marker states decode the name from layer 0; a one-direction probe erasure changed nothing but was weaker than a random edit. Copying layers 0-13 or 14-27 of a name-randomised sibling into a fine-tune recovers 66% and 65% (v1); 21% and 45% (pair A) of its shortcut reduction. 9 of the 12 predictions we could score, written before running, failed. Head sweeps cover 5 of 5 checkpoints; data are synthetic and LLM-labelled; one architecture.

title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild
abstract: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.

title: Spatial Prototype and Multiscale Expert Multiple-Instance Learning for Breast Cancer Subtype Prediction
abstract: Breast cancer subtype prediction from whole-slide images (WSIs) remains difficult because subtype morphology overlaps, class imbalance can bias training, and conventional multiple-instance learning (MIL) may discard relationships between neighboring patches. Evidence captured at one patch-aggregation scale may also be insufficient for every patient. We propose Spatial Prototype and Multiscale Expert Multiple-Instance Learning (SPME-MIL) for patient-level prediction of four PAM50 subtypes. SPME-MIL combines prototype-based patch aggregation, a global K-means cluster representation, and features that describe spatial relationships between neighboring patches. A WSI-level adaptation of the Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique (SMOTE) augments the less frequent classes. Using patch coordinates, we average neighboring patch features to form three aggregation scales. The Hybrid classifier conditionally refines Luminal A/B predictions from a main model. The Cascade classifier first separates Luminal from Non-Luminal tumors, then predicts the subtype within the selected group. A patient-level prediction rule selects one of their subtype probability vectors. On the held-out test set, SPME-MIL achieved an accuracy of 0.6933 and a macro-F1 score of 0.6035. The prediction rule increased macro-F1 by 0.0651 over the stronger individual classifier. SPME-MIL also achieved the highest patient-level metrics among eight adapted baseline pipelines evaluated with identical features and the same patient split; the highest baseline macro-F1 was 0.4202.

title: SRCWDNet: Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network for Multi-Label Remote Sensing Scene Classification
abstract: Multi-label remote sensing scene classification remains a challenging task due to complex spatial-spectral patterns, extreme class imbalance, and inter-label dependencies that are often insufficiently modeled. To address these challenges, we introduce a Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network (SRCWDNet), which integrates three key modules: (1) a Cross-Window Attention module that captures local and global visual context through learnable global tokens; (2) a Dual Label-Graph module that adaptively combines statistical co-occurrence graphs and learned semantic-embedding graphs to facilitate label-relational reasoning; and (3) a Neural Classifier Chain that sequentially predicts labels to exploit inter-label dependencies. Evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and trained with an Asymmetric-Graph-Consistency loss, SRCWDNet achieves accuracies of 98.93% and 96.53%, with corresponding F1-scores of 0.9365 and 0.8723 on the MLRSNet and China-MAS50k datasets, respectively, outperforming CNN, transformer, and lightweight baselines. These findings demonstrate that jointly modeling visual attention and adaptive label correlations can substantially improve multi-label remote sensing scene classification, particularly under long-tailed class distributions.

evidence.title: SRCWDNet: Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network for Multi-Label Remote Sensing Scene Classification
evidence.abstract: Multi-label remote sensing scene classification remains a challenging task due to complex spatial-spectral patterns, extreme class imbalance, and inter-label dependencies that are often insufficiently modeled. To address these challenges, we introduce a Semantic-Relational Cross-Window Dual-Graph Network (SRCWDNet), which integrates three key modules: (1) a Cross-Window Attention module that captures local and global visual context through learnable global tokens; (2) a Dual Label-Graph module that adaptively combines statistical co-occurrence graphs and learned semantic-embedding graphs to facilitate label-relational reasoning; and (3) a Neural Classifier Chain that sequentially predicts labels to exploit inter-label dependencies. Evaluated using five-fold cross-validation and trained with an Asymmetric-Graph-Consistency loss, SRCWDNet achieves accuracies of 98.93% and 96.53%, with corresponding F1-scores of 0.9365 and 0.8723 on the MLRSNet and China-MAS50k datasets, respectively, outperforming CNN, transformer, and lightweight baselines. These findings demonstrate that jointly modeling visual attention and adaptive label correlations can substantially improve multi-label remote sensing scene classification, particularly under long-tailed class distributions.

title: A Pipeline-Parallel System for Depth-Recurrent Models
abstract: Depth-recurrent (Looped) models raise effective depth by applying a shared stack of blocks several times. Scaling them usually requires pipeline parallelism, but commonly used interleaved 1F1B is drawn for an acyclic stage graph in which each micro-batch enters each stage once. Once that stack is split across stages, the same stage is visited several times on one micro-batch and later stages feed earlier ones: native 1F1B has no slot for the extra visit, cannot rank a first iteration against a second, and its neighbour-only send/receive order has no back edge to the first stage, so the arrangement stalls or fires out of order. We present Loop-PP, which rebuilds both the timetable and the communication for this cyclic layout. It schedules different iterations of the same stage separately, specializes a 1F1B skeleton into a globally consistent order over those visits, and emits a static instruction stream per rank that separates posting from waiting so communication overlaps local compute. Loop-PP is bit-identical to a single-stage reference. On 8B-60B MoE models, it lowers peak memory by as much as 32.8\%, and with compute budget fixed, the best observed throughput rises by 12.7\%.

title: Transformations of Managerial Leadership in the Era of Generative AI in Decision Making, Accountability, and Strategic Capability Development
abstract: The rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has significantly transformed how organizations manage information, develop strategic alternatives, and support managerial decision-making, shifting leadership responsibilities from information gathering toward directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs. This transformation raises critical questions concerning the boundaries of human and machine authority, accountability for AI-assisted decisions, and the strategic capabilities required for responsible AI integration. This study aimed to examine the transformation of managerial leadership in AI-assisted decision-making, identify key dimensions of managerial accountability, and synthesize the strategic capabilities necessary for responsible technology integration. A qualitative approach employing an integrative literature review was adopted, drawing on peer-reviewed journal articles, academic books, and official documents published primarily between 2020 and 2026. The selected literature was analyzed through thematic coding and critical comparative analysis. The findings indicated that managerial leadership evolved around three interrelated functions: directing, evaluating, and integrating AI-generated outputs, rather than simply experiencing a reduction in responsibilities through automation. Managerial accountability encompassed four dimensions: clear allocation of responsibility, transparency and traceability, meaningful human oversight, and risk management. These dimensions provided a conceptual basis for maintaining human accountability in AI-assisted decision-making. Furthermore, five strategic capabilities were identified as central to responsible AI integration: AI literacy, knowledge integration, governance capabilities, strategic adaptability, and organizational learning. The study concluded that managerial leadership transformation in the era of generative AI depended not merely on technological adoption but also on the integration of human judgment, robust accountability mechanisms, and adaptive strategic capabilities. These findings contributed to a conceptual framework for responsible AI governance and sustainable organizational adaptation.

title: Serialization and the Character-System: Measuring Narrative Concentration in French Fiction (1800--1940)
abstract: Every novel divides a finite quantity of narrative attention among its characters, and whether the shape of that division, between a narrative organized around a single figure and one spread across a crowd, has a history is far less settled than the abundance of critical commentary on protagonists might suggest. We operationalize Woloch's notion of the character-system, the distribution of narrative attention across a novel's cast structured by the tension between "the one" and "the many", as the inequality (Gini coefficient) of the PageRank distribution over a character network. We trace this measure of structural concentration across 12,011 French novels published between 1800 and 1940, drawn from the Hors d'usage corpus of Gallica fiction. Over the long nineteenth century the trajectory is U-shaped, with concentration declining to a trough in the 1850s-1860s and rising again through the turn of the century. The change is small, comparable to the difference between a novel built on two co-equal protagonists and one built on a single protagonist, but it is robust to the character cutoff, corpus density, cast size, and author effects. Detective and adventure fiction are less concentrated than the average novel of their period. Literary history reads the roman-feuilleton either as the novel of a superior hero or as a form of proliferating episodes, and on this structural measure our results support the second reading. Across the age of the feuilleton (1840-1914), authors whose careers were structured by newspaper serialization distribute centrality more evenly than a literary control, net of period, genre, and canon. Because such claims are only as trustworthy as the networks they rest on, we also evaluate the extraction pipeline against manually annotated novels, at the levels of cast and character identity.

title: Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting
abstract: 4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1-3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast. Code and models: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld. Project page: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld

title: Data and code for Evaluating Language Model Workflows for Collocations and Lexico-Grammatical Patterns
abstract: Recorded analytical data, saved numerical results and offline replay code for four language-model workflows retrieving collocations and lexico-grammatical patterns. The primary reference has 416 entries (271 collocations and 145 LGP families); the 417-entry reference is retained for sensitivity analysis. The package preserves accepted results, current manuscript figures, de-identified original paired coding categories and saved agreement summaries. It adds verbatim displayed-table extracts and documentation without new experiments, human coding, adjudication or statistical analysis.

title: Genome-to-Image Translation: Reconstructing Escherichia coli Morphology from Genomic Sequences
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance in Escherichia coli is established in routine practice by culture-based susceptibility testing, which is slow relative to the clinical need for an early treatment decision. Resistance status also leaves a measurable trace in cell morphology, and whole-genome sequencing of clinical isolates is increasingly available, which raises the question of whether colony appearance can be predicted directly from an isolate's genome. We formulate this as a conditional image-generation problem. The assembled contigs of each isolate are encoded into a single 768-dimensional vector by a frozen genomic language model through a segment-contig-isolate aggregation hierarchy, and a conditional Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty synthesizes colony images from this embedding together with the applied antibiotic and the resistance label. We train on 167,356 single-cell images from 22 clinical blood isolates imaged under azithromycin, ciprofloxacin, tetracycline, and a no-drug control, compare seven pretrained convolutional backbones inside the generator, and select ConvNeXt-Tiny on distributional image-quality metrics. The synthetic images are then assessed extrinsically: added to a reduced real training set, they improve per-antibiotic resistance classification, with a significant gain in resistant-class recall.

title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
abstract: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

title: Evaluating Chunking Strategies for Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Homogeneous Academic Documents
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) improves the factual reliability of large language models by combining generative capabilities with external knowledge retrieval. While extensively studied in open-domain and heterogeneous corpora, RAG’s performance in highly homogeneous and structured domains, such as institutional academic documents, remains underexplored. These document types are often lengthy, redundant, and formatted according to rigid institutional standards, posing unique challenges for information retrieval and semantic segmentation. This study systematically evaluates chunking strategies for RAG pipelines applied to Indonesian higher education documents, including curricula, syllabi, academic guidelines, and standard operating procedures. We compare fixed-length token-based chunking with varying sizes and overlaps to structure-based chunking aligned with logical document sections. All documents were preprocessed, embedded using IndoBERT-based sentence transformers, and indexed in ChromaDB. Retrieval effectiveness was assessed using Precision@k, Recall@k, and Mean Reciprocal Rank (MRR) with curated academic queries. Results indicate that smaller fixed-length chunks achieve higher top-1 precision, whereas structure-based chunks maintain semantic coherence and deliver superior recall across top-k retrieval. Integrating these retrieval strategies with LLaMA 3.2 and a Telegram bot demonstrates practical usability, providing accurate, context-grounded responses in real time. These findings highlight the critical role of chunking and top-k selection in optimizing RAG performance for structured, redundant academic corpora and offer guidance for designing knowledge management systems in higher education.

title: JONES-19: A Cultural Image Dataset Based on The Grammar of Ornament
abstract: We introduce JONES-19, a high-quality image dataset documenting 1,901 ornament designs belonging to nineteen human cultures. The images and their annotations are based on an open access archive of The Grammar of Ornament (London, 1856), by Owen Jones. The dataset poses numerous challenges as a benchmark for computer vision classification tasks and for research at the intersection of machine learning and art and design: a small sample size, image samples of human-designed artifacts rather than common objects in-context or natural scenes, imbalanced class distribution, and image distinctions based on fine details involving line patterns, reliefs, and colors. As a design-inspired dataset, JONES-19 can serve as a benchmark for various research fields, such as visual recognition, data-efficient learning, art-historical research, architectural style analysis, and cultural heritage. This paper describes the curation of the JONES-19 dataset and reports a baseline classification benchmark that evaluates the suitability of the dataset for training classifiers and exposes insights into inter-class relationships--particularly cultural similarities--by examining patterns in misclassification errors. The dataset and its accompanying documentation are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/harvardseas-cultural-ornaments/JONES-19.

title: CrownFusion: 3D Dental Crown Generation Using Geometry Images and Latent Diffusion
abstract: We introduce CrownFusion, a latent diffusion model to generate 3D dental crown designs from geometry images, a 2D-grid encoding of surface coordinates. Departing from traditional approaches that use point clouds, our "CrownImage" representation not only unlocks the full power of image-based generative architectures, but also preserves fine geometric detail by operating at far higher spatial resolutions than point clouds to alleviate smoothing artifacts in the 3D generation. Conditioned on jointly learned embeddings of the surrounding dentition, our probabilistic diffusion model produces anatomically plausible crowns with morphological variations tailored to individual patient cases. To accommodate multiple valid designs, we propose an occlusal fit metric based on proximity to the antagonist teeth. We evaluate our method through quantitative experiments and qualitative studies involving expert testimonials. We also release the FDI 16 Crown Dataset, comprising 11,513 annotated intra-oral scans, to support future research in dental CAD.

title: DexDuet: Learning Contact-Preserving Bimanual Dexterity from Human Demonstrations
abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/

title: Construct Emergence Tracing: From Meaning to Mechanism in Transformer Interpretability via Generative Psychometrics
abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) allow researchers and practitioners to develop and deploy systems that perform impressive feats such as generating coherent texts and answering questions across various domains. Yet, there is currently an interpretability problem regarding the internal representation of multidimensional psychological constructs (e.g., personality traits) throughout multiple layers of deep neural networks. Here, we propose Construct Emergence Tracing (CET), a novel methodology to address this problem. CET utilizes ideas from Generative Psychometrics to trace the emergence of concepts from high-level meaning to underlying mechanisms. CET consists of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis combined with three complementary indices reflecting the quality of representation (semantic coherence via normalized mutual information; NMI, entropy-based organization structure via Total Entropy Fit Index; TEFI, and topological compressibility via a compression-based proxy for Kolmogorov Complexity; KC). CET also computes a weighted composite of the above three indices in order to derive a metric named Representational Maturity (RM). We applied CET to fourteen LM models ranging from nominal sizes of 117 million to 32 billion parameters. We utilized a fixed design of five items per attribute representing the five attributes of grandiose narcissism and yielded a total of 9,801,000 network estimates across recorded states, embedding dimensions, and repeated item samples. Results show that across architectures construct recovery generally increases from early to intermediate states. However, its initiation, amplitude, alignment with different metrics, and termination vary considerably across models. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct, overall mean NMI followed a monotonic increase based on nominal model size from 0.504 (0.5B) to 0.653 (32B). This trend did not replicate for selected peak values or output layer retention. Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

title: Data-Driven Identification of Uncertainty Sets with Conformance Guarantees
abstract: Formal verification and controller synthesis require accurate models. Conformance relations specify the required accuracy of a model such that properties established for the model carry over to the target system. Existing methods for establishing them from measured data are typically restricted to a single relation, a specific model class, or a downstream verification algorithm. We present ConfID, a unified framework that establishes reachset, trace, and simulation conformance with respect to measured traces by identifying uncertainty sets for a given, possibly nonlinear nominal model. Unmodeled effects are thus captured by nondeterminism rather than by refining the nominal dynamics. For all three conformance relations, the identification is a linear program that minimizes the size of the reachable sets; only its constraints depend on the relation. We further derive distribution-free bounds on the probability that the identified models are conformant for unseen behaviors. Experiments on simulated and real-world data evaluate the models identified for the three relations, confirm the guarantees, and show that these models cover unseen behaviors more reliably than baselines, with comparable or smaller sets.

title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

title: ToolResult-800: Counterfactual Tool-Observation Dataset, 800 Frozen Prefixes
abstract: ToolResult-800 v1.0.2 is a fixed-prefix counterfactual dataset for measuring whether the content of a real tool observation changes a language-model agent's next decision. v1.0.2 is a path-leak errata release: it supersedes v1.0.1 (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.24449467), whose distributed copies exposed absolute build-machine and server paths. Contents. 800 primary + 80 reserve tau-bench prefixes (400 airline, 400 retail); five observation arms (verbatim scrubbed JSON V; faithful prose s=0; one non-critical change s=1; one critical wrong value s=2; critical wrong value plus contradiction s=3); frozen perturbation records; scrubbed decision, recovery, and jitter ledgers from three open-weight 8-9B models (21,611 confirmatory generations); audit packets and sheets; all analysis JSONs behind the paper's 11 main and 14 supplementary tables; the exploratory second-renderer artifact (2,250 generations on 150 prefixes) with its three ledgers; the parser-v4 rescore and second-renderer code; the preregistration and amendments A-001-A-011; a table-to-artifact map, checksums, a one-command validator (19/19 L1; 25/25 with six CPU-only producer reruns), and path_rescan.json. Path-leak fix. The v1.0.1 archive contained 16 absolute paths in 8 files: the repository root in labels/g0_report.md and four analysis JSONs, and the server home directory prefix in labels/g1_calibration_v3.json. The v1.0.2 builder replaces repository roots, server home prefixes, and drive-rooted paths with [repo] in every staged text file before checksums are written; path_rescan.json records the counts and 0 residual hits. The generated source artifacts are unchanged; only the released copies are scrubbed. Result. Confirmatory analysis complete and unchanged: pooled conditional-logit slope 0.877 [0.770, 0.998] with three failed gate criteria (parser 1.55% vs 1%; severity s2/s3 88.3% vs 90%; crude recovery on the semantic risk set 24.4/32.9/21.3% vs 50%). Measurement framing; no causal or content-sensitivity claim. The second-renderer check is exploratory and is never pooled with the confirmatory estimate. Licenses. Project data additions: CC BY 4.0. Repository code: MIT. Upstream tau-bench: MIT, notices preserved. No raw trajectories, PII, weights, caches, or credentials are included; the distributed copy is PII-redacted and path-scrubbed at build time. Reproducibility. Code: github.com/Atik203/tool-observation. Frozen manifest SHA-256: d6e034d7f1132b314ad1f82bf14faa0f6762975ee7b404b54cc365acfac5487a. Concept DOI (all versions): 10.5281/zenodo.24449466. This record contains ToolResult-800-v1.0.2.zip (SHA-256 e63e0c1313e15095619fad7950fd82291ed8b681bdcd961ef7e3a6b4d96ca113) and SHA256SUMS (SHA-256 c0bc4fd52447861fc904006054339ab057f4df7d813f0ac7967f8f99c10cd902). The archive expands to 137 checksummed files plus SHA256SUMS and release_record.json (139 files); every entry was re-checked against SHA256SUMS after upload, with 0 mismatches. title: Do learned image captioning metrics generalize? Auditing duplicated samples in human-judgment benchmarks
abstract: Learned image captioning metrics are trained and tested on human judgments, so their reported correlation is a claim about generalization. We audit this claim for the three most recent collections of such judgments, Polaris, Nebula, and Spica, matching images at the pixel level. First, test samples reappear in training sets: the Spica training set contains about two-thirds of the Polaris test set, with identical human ratings. Second, controlled retraining shows that duplicates can inflate a metric: for Pearl, the gain is confined to the duplicated samples and grows with every epoch; for DENEB, it stays below one point. The gain depends on the learner and on how often a training set repeats a sample. Third, Kendall's τ over all samples is the sum of two terms, detecting captions with the lowest human score and ranking the others; the first supplies most of the reported correlation and is nearly saturated. The recent test sets cannot order Polos, DENEB and Pearl consistently, and a ridge regression on frozen features matches or exceeds all three. Fourth, we propose a protocol that ranks a learned metric only with a model trained without test samples, reports both terms, and compares metrics by paired tests. Under it, zero-shot vision--language judges rank first on the three recent test sets, and a fine-tuned judge ranks first on the three earlier benchmarks. The same analysis applies to any evaluator learned from human judgments; filter lists and code are released at https://github.com/morninghut/ic-dataset-audit .

title: GHOST - General meta-Heuristic Optimization Solving Toolkit
abstract: GHOST (General meta-Heuristic Optimization Solving Toolkit) is a C++20 library to let a user declare his or her own combinatorial problems. It implements a meta-heuristic solver aiming to solve any kind of combinatorial and optimization problems declared in Constraint Programming. GHOST allows the user to easily declare problems in different Constraint Programming formalisms such as Constraint Satisfaction Problems (CSP), Constrained Optimization Problems (COP), Error Function-based Constraint Satisfaction Problems (EF-CSP), and Error Function-based Constrained Optimization Problems (EF-COP).

title: Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure for Subsurface Seepage Forecasting and Relief Placement
abstract: Truncating a large heterogeneous diffusion model around a localized, threshold-activated outlet saves degrees of freedom but severs exterior feedback that governs when the outlet opens and how much it discharges. By separating forcing-driven background head from local withdrawal drawdown, Site-Conditioned Boundary Closure (SCBC) maps local physical descriptors to positive exchange coefficients at the cut boundary. Supervised on unforced donor-domain withdrawal responses, these coefficients yield a passivity-preserving reduced operator that generalizes across unseen forcing histories without refitting. We evaluate SCBC on flood-driven subsurface seepage beneath levee foundations against full-grid reference simulations (MODFLOW~6). Across three held-out foundation panels, a single frozen SCBC tree estimator reduced peak-discharge log RMSE by 26.1%, 30.9% and 42.6% relative to identical local patches using a shared boundary coefficient. We then test whether better screening forecasts improve constrained placement, minimizing peak landside toe head subject to a discharge capacity limit and a budget of three sequential full-grid checks. On a separate 36-foundation test using a coarser 30-state ring operator, a neural SCBC estimator improved discharge forecasts across candidates yet selected four over-capacity placements before checks, compared with one for a shared-coefficient ring, which recovered all 144 reference optima after three checks.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
abstract: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: How Organizational AI Ethics Governance Shapes Employee Creativity: A Conceptual Analysis of Mechanisms and Boundary Conditions
abstract: As AI becomes embedded in organizational decision-making and knowledge production, employees gain new tools for accessing and generating information while also confronting concerns about algorithmic evaluation, data use, and accountability. Drawing on research on AI ethics, algorithmic management, and organizational creativity, this conceptual study defines organizational AI ethics governance as the rules, procedures, and allocation of responsibilities that guide the development, deployment, operation, and retirement of AI systems. We argue that such governance can shape employee creativity through several connected mechanisms. Fair and contestable procedures can strengthen procedural justice, while transparent system boundaries and meaningful human review can support calibrated trust. Tolerance for responsible experimentation, together with discretion over how AI is used, can protect psychological safety and job autonomy. Governance also determines whether human–AI collaboration broadens exploration or channels employees toward standardized outputs. These effects depend on task characteristics, the stakes of AI-assisted decisions, whether AI is used primarily for automation or augmentation, employees' AI literacy, and the consistency between formal rules and managerial conduct. This study suggests that organizations should translate ethical principles into risk-based review, purpose limitation in data use, effective contestability and appeal mechanisms, employee participation, and oversight across the AI system life cycle so that AI can serve as a resource for careful creative work rather than a substitute for judgment.

title: Self-Upgrading Embodied Agents
abstract: An embodied agent built on a language model goes to work with the weights it was given and keeps them for life. To get better, it needs more training, or reflection, memory, search or prompts that cost every step and are lost when the task changes. Editing weights by reasoning, weight-space programming, could end this, but has stayed with models that only reason or relied on a far larger commercial model. We introduce the self-upgrading embodied agent, to our knowledge the first that learns from its own experience by upgrading its own weights on the job, between its tasks, with no training, no gradient, no reward model, no second model, no test-time scaling and no harness or prompt engineering. By day a 27B agent works in a household environment. At night it reads its record, finds many of its steps wasted on replies that reach the token limit before any action, traces the habit to one direction in its hidden states, and rewrites one tensor of its weights. An agent that rewrites itself must first never break itself, so it is its own examiner: it tests every change against its unchanged self on practice tasks and keeps only what holds. When an edit holds, the next day it is a better agent, at the same cost per step: over thousands of held-out episodes, 48 fresh seeds a task, its one kept edit makes it complete significantly more tasks, in fewer steps, with fewer wasted and fewer tokens. This self-improvement is multi-round, stable and continual: through the nights that follow, the upgrade holds, without collapse. Of four sizes of its family, only the 27B agent does this. From here on, an embodied agent need not keep training and inference apart: as it works, it gathers its own experience and upgrades itself, with no separate pre-training or post-training and no human intervention. We believe this opens lifelong continual learning for robots: stable, continual, recursive self-improvement.

title: Target-Part Preference Optimization for Part-Aware 3D Generation
abstract: Part-aware 3D generation requires not only globally plausible objects but also complete, well-separated semantic parts, yet high-quality part decompositions remain too scarce to support large-scale supervised fine-tuning. We study whether preference fine-tuning based on Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) can adapt a pretrained part-aware generator from limited part-annotated data without architectural changes. We rank candidates generated with different random seeds against ground-truth (GT) geometric metrics, and select the (object, target-part) examples with the largest across-seed quality gap. Each selected example stores a seed pair whose two flow trajectories share one clean GT compositional latent and differ only in Gaussian noise. We derive a reference-relative target-block preference loss from FlowDPO that compares the two trajectories against a frozen reference model. GT flow-matching losses on the target block and complete part set provide absolute supervision, while only the diffusion transformer (DiT) is updated. Human-ranked controls test an alternative ordering source, and synthetic cropping provides controlled loser targets that are incomplete by construction. Among the three training-set scales, the medium-scale setting gives the strongest result on held-out Objaverse and outperforms both the pretrained generator and the reported direct supervised fine-tuning baseline on the multi-part aggregate. Further analysis shows sensitivity to pair ordering, target-part coverage, and the balance between pairwise and GT supervision. Cross-dataset experiments show less consistent gains under distribution shift.

title: When Does Reasoning Help Entity Disambiguation? Small LLMs In-Domain and Under Shift
abstract: Entity disambiguation (mapping ambiguous mentions in text to entities in a knowledge base) is a foundational step in tasks such as knowledge graph construction, question answering, and information extraction. Recent work has applied LLMs to this problem, achieving stateof-the-art performance. Notably, reasoning LLMs have been shown to perform entity disambiguation in a true zero-shot fashion, generalizing across knowledge bases and domains. However, it is unclear whether this capability survives, or remains competitive, with smaller LLMs, where entity disambiguation has typically relied on reranking rather than reasoning. We ask when reasoning is worth its cost at small scale. We compare pointwise, listwise, and reasoning-based candidate-selection components within a classical coarse-to-fine entity disambiguation pipeline, across the classical, few-shot and true zero-shot settings. The reasoning paradigm is trained with distillation and reinforcement learning recipes. The benefit of reasoning grows with domain shift: negligible in-domain, decisive in the true zero-shot setting. We show that two distinct factors are at work: the reranker's uncertainty over the candidates locates where the paradigms disagree, while shift governs which is right when they do.

title: Attention Temperature Confounds Zero-Shot Context Extension
abstract: A training-time attention change is usually judged for zero-shot context extension against a dense baseline beyond the training length at the default temperature, $τ= 1$. The outcome depends on how miscalibrated the baseline is there: the share of perplexity it recovers when its logits are sharpened by one scalar. Under the standard recipe (fp32 master weights), an 8k-trained baseline is 8-15% miscalibrated at 30k in three seed-paired 365M twins; in one of them this makes the block-sparse-trained twin look 7% better, which calibration removes. In pure-bf16 training without master weights the miscalibration is several times larger: an AdamW step ($β_2 = 0.95$) on a gain initialised at 1.0 is below half the bf16 spacing at peak learning rates under $1.7\times10^{-3}$, so gains never move (22 checkpoints), the baseline is 37-58% miscalibrated, and block-sparse pretraining, attention dropout and ALiBi look 6-35% better. Calibrating one temperature per model and length removes all three advantages, leaves ALiBi 5% behind RoPE and keeps part of the gain of a positive control, NTK-aware scaling. Unfreezing the gains reverses the block-sparse advantage at 365M and removes 71-89% of it at 1.2B. We recommend reporting extension results at calibrated temperatures and checking that normalisation gains moved.

title: Accuracy Is Not Evidence: Measuring and Training Evidence Dependence in Video Temporal Grounding
abstract: In video temporal grounding, a correct interval can come from finding the event, answering blind or fitting one annotation style, and Recall at IoU scores them alike. We measure evidence dependence, how much the answer rests on the event's frames. Our fixed-answer audit edits either the frames inside the annotated interval or, as a placebo, as many frames elsewhere in the same video, and compares the two drops in the annotated answer's likelihood. Supervised fine-tuning and three public checkpoints trained with IoU-reward reinforcement learning raise the accuracy of Qwen2.5-VL-7B by 9 to 20 points, partly by answering blind and by fitting one annotation. Yet their answers rest on the event no more than the base model's, and the same holds for IoU-reward training on our data at the audit's frame rate. This comparison is a difference of the model's own likelihoods, so we can train on it. A placebo contrast and a bound on the placebo drop rule out learning to react to any edit. With them, evidence dependence rises in all five base models we train, and the weight on clean supervision controls how much. Added to IoU-reward training, the objective raises evidence dependence while keeping the accuracy gain. Masking the event's frames makes the trained models decline or miss the event more often than their base; masking as many other frames does not. The dependence moves to another event when the query names it, and holds on a second dataset and under patch scrambling, an edit never used in training.

title: Look Back, Draft Ahead: Corrective Prefix Attention for Parallel Speculative Decoding
abstract: Parallel speculative decoders propose an entire token block at once, yet one early inconsistency can cause the target to reject its remaining suffix. We introduce Corrective Prefix Attention (CPA), which combines prefix-aware selection with autoregressive supervision to improve these parallel drafts. CPA lets each candidate attend to earlier choices within the block. Fixed candidate shortlists allow all pairwise interactions to be computed before selection, reducing the sequential walk to table lookups, accumulation and lightweight scoring rather than repeated neural evaluations. An auxiliary autoregressive loss trains the shared backbone on clean prefixes without adding an inference pass. Across eight math, code and dialogue benchmarks with Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B targets on Ascend NPUs, CPA commits 13--15\% more tokens per verification round than DSpark and 25--26\% more than DFlash. Its mean speedups reach $3.35\times$ and $3.37\times$ under greedy decoding and $2.86\times$ under sampling for both targets. Ablations support both components, while capacity sweeps demonstrate that greater acceptance alone does not guarantee faster decoding. These results motivate correcting parallel proposals with causal information while keeping sequential computation inexpensive.

title: MMMem: Self-Improving Agents with Task-Aware Multimodal Experience Consolidation
abstract: AI agents accumulate conversations, images, and documents through long-term interactions with users. Answering later questions often requires connecting evidence across these records, yet the resulting understanding is rarely retained, allowing mistakes to recur on related questions. Existing multimodal memory methods largely focus on storing and retrieving records, with limited mechanisms for learning from completed tasks and consolidating task-specific experience. We therefore propose MMMem, a task-aware multimodal memory framework that extracts and consolidates experience from completed tasks through four complementary strategies. First, source-linked multi-view memory organizes original text, images, and rendered pages alongside generated scene images that combine clues across records for retrieval. Second, source-generated tasks support knowledge alignment at two levels: warm-up consolidates source knowledge into task-relevant experiences in external memory, while self-training adapts the model's parametric knowledge to task demands. Third, the same vision-language model distills completed tasks into experiences that record the task context, conclusion, and support links. Finally, task-aware retrieval recalls source views and relevant experiences for answering and verification, while source-supported reuse guides long-term retention. Across three memory benchmarks and two vision-language readers, MMMem outperforms eight baselines. With Qwen3.5-9B, MMMem achieves relative gains of 36.9%, 17.6%, and 15.2% over the best-performing baselines on LoCoMo, Mem-Gallery, and LooGLE v2, respectively. Ablations show consistent gains from training and memory warm-up, while case studies illustrate how individual components work in practice.

title: Quantum Science and Technologies: From Strangeness to Opportunities
abstract: Quantum physics has already shaped our daily lives through a first technological revolution: semiconductors, transistors, lasers, atomic clocks, medical imaging, and modern electronics. This first revolution primarily exploits the collective and statistical behavior of large ensembles of particles. A second revolution is now underway: it consists in controlling individual quantum systems by exploiting superposition, entanglement, interference, and measurement, while mastering decoherence. This transition opens perspectives in four major technological pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. The presentation assesses the maturity of these four pillars: quantum sensing and metrology, quantum communication, quantum simulation, and quantum computing. Particular attention is given to full-stack hardware architecture, to the distinction between physical and logical qubits, and to that between quantum advantage and fault tolerance. The presentation also addresses AI–quantum interactions, distinguishing operational AI-for-quantum methods from quantum-for-AI research and its structural limitations. It concludes with practical resources, cloud access, career pathways, and a perspective on skills, access, and post-quantum cryptography priorities. Keywords: quantum computing; quantum sensing; quantum communication; quantum simulation; post-quantum cryptography; quantum error correction; quantum machine learning, quantum software tools.

title: Preflight: Agentic Last-Mile Verification for AI Software Supply Chains
abstract: Software dependencies execute within the trust boundary of downstream applications, yet provenance, static analysis, and package-level behavioral approaches do not directly determine how a released artifact behaves for a specific program. We present Preflight, a program-scoped pre-execution verifier for Python dependencies that extracts application-referenced symbols, iteratively synthesizes and validates function-level harnesses, executes resolved artifacts in a restricted environment, records behavioral fingerprints, and compares target behavior against prior versions when suitable baselines exist. We evaluate Preflight on four real software-supply-chain incidents under five application contexts, a 100-package benign corpus, and a controlled function-level versus import-only ablation. Preflight returns malicious verdicts in four incident contexts and a clean verdict in the LiteLLM client context, where the affected proxy-server path is not exercised. All 100 evaluated benign packages receive clean verdicts, with zero observed false positives. In a controlled ablation on Ultralytics and ctx, function-level harnesses expose malicious behavior in both incidents, whereas import-only probing exposes neither. Together, these results show that conditioning behavioral verification on the downstream program can expose security-relevant dependency behavior while remaining selective on benign workloads.

title: Innata-0: A Native Embodied World System with Model-Agent Co-Design
abstract: The physical world is open-ended, dynamic, and partially observable. While foundation models have advanced embodied intelligence, standalone models struggle with long-horizon execution, and simply integrating models with agents may lead to inconsistencies between planning and physical control. To support reliable and adaptive behaviors in the physical world, we introduce Innata-0, a native embodied world system. Innata-0 jointly designs an embodied world-action model and an agent to combine their complementary strengths. The model, Innata-0-WAM, adopts a tri-tower Mixture-of-Transformers architecture that integrates understanding, prediction, and action generation. The agent, Innata-0-Agent, coordinates long-horizon execution through memory, verification, and recovery. A co-design protocol is further proposed to align model training with agent execution and leverage validated experiences to support subsequent adaptation and model improvement. Extensive evaluations demonstrate strong embodied capabilities across understanding, world prediction, and robotic manipulation. Innata-0 represents our first step toward physical intelligence, and we see it as the beginning of a much longer journey.

title: LiveLoRA: Exact KV Cache Migration Across LoRA Updates for LLM Agents
abstract: Updating an LLM adapter should not require replaying the full interaction history of every active session. Yet reusing key-value (KV) cache entries computed under an earlier version mixes model versions, while full-history re-prefill becomes increasingly costly as histories and session fleets grow. We introduce LiveLora, a model-runtime co-design for exact final-block KV cache migration. Frozen lower decoder blocks and fixed K/V adapter down-projections preserve each token's base projections and low-rank coordinates across adapter versions. The runtime reconstructs candidate K/V, reevaluates the latest token through the final block, and commits the adapter, cache, and next-token logits together. We prove continuation equivalence to full-history re-prefill in exact arithmetic under the stated model assumptions. On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, median paired publication speedups over full-history re-prefill average $68.98\times$ across five runs for 32 active sessions with 8K tokens each. Serving benchmarks show approximately 4.8% decoding overhead relative to native cached decoding. Compared with retained-boundary replay, compact retention gives a $3.42\times$ reduction in additional session storage at 8K, with similar measured publication-plus-decoding cost. LiveLora allows persistent LLM agents to adopt new adapter versions without replaying their full interaction histories.

title: PixelOne: From Options to Pixels in a Single Forward for GUI Grounding
abstract: GUI grounding requires precise clicks at low latency. Recent models such as GUI-Decisions and GUI-Swift predict coordinates in one forward pass using fixed global bins with local refinement. However, screenshot downsampling removes detail needed to locate small controls, while fixed bins cover larger pixel ranges at higher resolutions. We introduce PixelOne, which transfers spatial knowledge from a search teacher to a student that predicts clicks directly from screenshots at native resolution. The teacher uses VideoJEV's text-option scorer to select rows and columns and progressively zoom into candidate regions. The student inherits the teacher's parameters and matches its distributions over explored regions through spatial distillation alongside box supervision. At inference, the same decision head selects a visual token, and a lightweight pixel head predicts the click within it, all in one forward pass. A click-aligned loss encourages pixels inside the target box to score above those outside. Across four benchmarks, PixelOne-Pro-35B-A3B achieves 83.8% mean accuracy, the highest among the evaluated single-forward grounders, with a mean latency of 0.43 s per target.

title: SayWhen: Set-Valued Semantic Commitment for Low-Regret Early Speech
abstract: Speaking early turns a prediction into an irreversible public commitment. We introduce SayWhen, a test-time controller that selects a task-directed act shared across typed continuation plans and controls its release as speech. A persistent veto blocks playback when intervening transcripts invalidate the candidate. We define regret-free early speech (RFES) to measure supported pre-endpoint releases without scored incompatibility. On a 72-prefix branching diagnostic, the generated-plan frontier attains 6.0% RFES with zero observed mean regret, versus 8.2% RFES and 0.068 regret for Matched Top-One. Measured planner latency constrains this path; a deterministic retail schema attains 31.7% RFES, compared with 32.0% for the complete policy. In a separate 30-task $τ$-Voice simulation, schema-derived candidates with cached text-to-speech (TTS) audio attain 21/30 task-level RFES. Eligible audio begins 1.51 seconds before the user-audio endpoint among the 22 tasks with early speech, or 1.11 seconds over all 30 tasks with zero for tasks without eligible early speech. Semantic veto and endpoint waiting each pass 16/30 tasks. Together, the studies demonstrate a controlled coverage-compatibility trade-off and schema-based pre-endpoint operation, making the supported public commitment an explicit unit of voice-agent control.

title: RoomTokens: Masked Diffusion over Structured Tokens for Indoor Scene Synthesis
abstract: Generating 3D indoor scenes requires a representation that captures object semantics, instance identity, height structure, and orientation while respecting room geometry. Methods that model scenes as sequences of object vectors learn spatial constraints implicitly, leaving collisions and boundary violations to losses or post-processing; semantic-map methods make occupancy explicit, but collapse instance and directional structure. We introduce RoomTokens, a sliced structured-token representation in which each token stores semantic class, instance-color identity, and facing field. This representation allows a scene to be generated as a discrete grid while preserving cues for instance grouping, orientation estimation, and 3D extent prediction. To learn the RoomToken distribution, we propose MDIRT (Masked Diffusion over RoomTokens), a masked discrete diffusion model that denoises semantic/instance-color/facing channels jointly with a shared cross-slice backbone. Architectural tokens are clamped as explicit floor- plan constraints, so the model samples furniture layouts that respect room geometry while retaining instance and object-attribute structure. Experiments on 3D-FRONT show that RoomTokens with MDIRT improve layout fidelity and physical consistency over sequence/vector- and map-based methods, suggesting structured spatial tokens as a practical choice for discrete 3D scene synthesis.

title: Gender and Agency in AI Career Guidance for Women: A Socio-Technical Audit of General-Purpose Language Models
abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. Studies of gender bias in large language model (LLM) career advice mostly score single outputs about a person described to the model. But career guidance is a conversation with the woman herself, in which the advice can end up making the decision for her or treat a barrier she faces as a lack of confidence. We report a preregistered socio-technical audit of the career guidance that ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude give women through their APIs. We scripted 34 multi-turn conversations grounded in research on women’s careers, ran each five times per system, and added male versions of 14 to test gender cues (972 conversations). Human raters scored 304 conversations on nine objectives drawn from that research and from coaching ethics, with a second rater and an expert adjudicator for disagreements. Failures to preserve her agency had the highest share for every system (36% to 50% of conversations scored 1 or above on a 0 to 3 scale) and were more frequent than gender bias failures. Gemini was more often sycophantic. Swapping the user's gender showed no systematic difference, but pair differences depended on how the name was given. No LLM judge agreed acceptably with human raters, and the human raters also often disagreed, so the rates are descriptive. Audits of AI career advice should use more than one gender cue and, because models change, be repeated over time. LLM judges can serve as a screening aid, but scoring needs two or more human experts.

title: NoveltyGate: Novelty, Not Error, Decides Which VLA Prefix Tokens to Compute Exactly
abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models such as $π_{0.5}$ re-encode the camera images and the instruction with a 2B-parameter backbone at every control step, and the feed-forward layers of this prefix account for most of its compute. A natural way to save this compute is to send most tokens through a low-rank MLP and compute exactly only the tokens whose approximation error is large. We find that this intuition is wrong. Even a verifier that knows every token's exact error picks the wrong tokens, producing 1.3--1.7$\times$ larger action deviation than a simple test of whether a token's input is novel, that is, whether it falls outside the subspace seen during calibration. Large errors concentrate in tokens the policy relies on little, such as the third-person camera, while the novelty test favors the wrist camera, a view the action depends on heavily. We call this the error--reliance gap. Building on it, we propose NoveltyGate, a training-free method that routes each prefix token, once per layer and before any multiplication, to either a low-rank or the original MLP. Deciding once per layer instead of once per matrix product avoids moving wide intermediate tensors and keeps every shape static, so the whole prefix runs as a single CUDA graph. On LIBERO, NoveltyGate accelerates the $π_{0.5}$ prefix by up to 1.61$\times$, stays 2.7--2.9$\times$ closer to the original policy than channel pruning and low-rank compression at equal compute, and preserves closed-loop task success.

title: What Makes Good Data for Training Coding Agents? A Systematic Study on SWE-Gym
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) trains coding agents on software tasks whose hidden tests decide the reward, yet task collections check these tests only against the reference fix. We ask what makes a task good training data, focusing on the correctness of its reward labels. We audit SWE-Gym with two LLM families, and a suspected error counts only if execution reproduces it. We find that unsolved often means mislabelled: 74% of the tasks that a 9B base model never solves have a test that rejects correct fixes (a false negative), versus 20% of those it sometimes solves. We repair or remove such tasks, and the audited tasks that remain train better policies. At equal size and matched difficulty, models trained on them score 2.4 and 2.7 points higher on held-out tasks from SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro than models trained on the original tasks, whereas simply dropping the never-solved tasks shows no such gain. We further find that wrong patches that pass (false positives) make up about a quarter of all passing patches, and that new tests that catch a quarter of them do not change held-out scores detectably. A pass rate shows whether a task yields reward, not whether that reward is right, so the reward labels themselves must be checked. To this end, we release SWE-Gym-Verified with its 1,087 audited tasks, every verdict with its executed evidence, our training sets, and the full audit pipeline.

title: Leakage-Safe Auditing of Attribution-Driven Data Curation in Medical Imaging
abstract: When can an attribution-derived anomaly justify changing a medical-imaging training set? We formulate attribution-driven curation as three separately testable claims: anomaly detection, harmfulness estimation, and intervention utility. We test the first and third using a patient-disjoint, identifier-preserving audit of a 3D convolutional classifier for computed tomography angiography aneurysm candidates. We identify 232 exactly zero-valued arrays among 1,201 positive patches, including 170 training positives, and invalidate a historical 321-patch attention-failure subgroup whose identifier-free records were joined to files by position. On the held-out test set, GradCAM++ spatial concentration is central for every candidate class, reversing the historical pattern. GradCAM++ and Integrated Gradients show negative rank-order agreement for positives, limiting method-independent anatomical interpretation. Across five paired training seeds, removing the 170 corrupted training positives yields AUC 0.9617 +/- 0.0044 versus 0.9652 +/- 0.0039 for full-data training (difference -0.0035; 95% CI -0.0082 to 0.0007). Excluding 34 raw-zero test positives widens rather than closes the gap, countering a blank-memorization explanation. Budget-matched random-removal controls suggest the result is not simply an effect of reducing training size. Input corruption does not necessarily imply that deletion improves generalization. Our framework makes leakage control, sample identity, and intervention testing explicit in attribution-driven medical-imaging data curation.

title: Quantizing in the Loop: Drift-Aware Ultra-Low-Bit Vision-Language-Action Models
abstract: Deploying large vision-language-action (VLA) models on resource-constrained robots demands extreme compression, yet existing post-training quantization (PTQ) methods frequently collapse at ultra-low bit-widths (le 2 bits). We trace this failure to two mismatches in standard pipelines. First, calibrating on static offline demonstrations induces distribution shift: minor quantization perturbations drive the policy into unseen states where uncalibrated errors compound. Second, minimizing the layer-wise weight reconstruction error is a flawed proxy, as action generation depends only on the representations consumed by the action head. We present LoopQ, an on-policy ultra-low-bit quantization framework. LoopQ closes the loop by calibrating on states from the quantized policy's own rollouts. It then adds readout-aligned fine-tuning, which freezes the trellis codes and optimizes only lightweight lookup tables and scaling factors to align the backbone readout with the full-precision teacher. With all linear layers at 2 bits, LoopQ achieves a 60.4% success rate on LIBERO-Plus with GR00T N1.7, close to the 61.8% of full precision. Even at 1 bit per weight, π_{0.5} still completes 80.0% of LIBERO tasks. With 8-bit activations, the 2-bit π_{0.5} runs on integer kernels on an embedded NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor, with 4.1times smaller weights and 44% less memory. On a real AgileX Piper arm, it stays within one success of full precision on each of three tasks. Code and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/ForeverBlue816/LoopQ
