title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. As AI also makes decisions about work allocation, we compare a set of LLMs. We find many models also deviate from purely objective decisions, particularly when the project stakes are low, but there is wide heterogeneity as to how much and in what manner they weigh enjoyment. These results raise questions about what role human experience may play in decisions around where and how to integrate AI into workplaces. Integration may be jagged across settings due to consideration not only of the relative capabilities of workers, but also the human experience of work, the valence of that experience (e.g., more strongly weighing aversion), the context (e.g., stakes), and who is making or guiding such choices (human or LLM).

title: PathStream: Towards Streaming Diagnostic Copilots for Whole-Slide Pathology
abstract: Pathologists reach a diagnosis by integrating morphological evidence across regions and magnifications along viewing trajectories. Existing pathology AI rarely reflects this process: models predict from selected image regions, answer questions within fixed visual contexts, or navigate slides autonomously. We formalize pathologist-led streaming diagnosis, in which the pathologist controls navigation while a copilot selectively describes incoming views and synthesizes accumulated evidence into a final diagnosis. We record five pathologists' viewing trajectories on 1,791 TCGA whole-slide images (WSIs) spanning ten organs, with response labels, morphological descriptions, and session-level findings and diagnoses. We construct PathStreamBench to assess response timing, morphological description, and session-level diagnosis, alongside auxiliary video understanding. We introduce PathStream, which jointly learns streaming responses and diagnosis through two-stage training, with a diagnosis-attention loss guiding attention during diagnosis to relevant visual and textual evidence accumulated as the examination unfolds. PathStream outperforms 14 vision-language models and three domain-fine-tuned baselines on the core tasks, achieving a trajectory WSI Relevance score of 77.87, surpassing the strongest domain-fine-tuned baseline's 62.76. Without additional training, its diagnostic capabilities generalize to new educational pathology videos, three external centers, and an unseen organ.

title: Persepsi Pengguna terhadap Kontribusi Sistem Informasi Bimbingan Konseling Berbasis Website dalam Mendukung Mutu Layanan di SMA Negeri 1 Banda Aceh
abstract: Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis persepsi pengguna terhadap kontribusi RuangSIBK, yaitu sistem informasi bimbingan dan konseling berbasis website, dalam mendukung mutu layanan bimbingan dan konseling di SMA Negeri 1 Banda Aceh. Fokus kajian dibatasi pada persepsi kontribusi sistem terhadap mutu layanan, bukan pembuktian peningkatan secara kausal. Penelitian merupakan evaluasi deskriptif dalam kerangka penelitian dan pengembangan dengan memanfaatkan data observasi, wawancara, validasi ahli, pengujian fungsional, dan angket skala Likert lima tingkat. Data respons peserta didik melibatkan 105 responden dari kelas terpilih. Hasil angket menunjukkan respons keseluruhan sebesar 82,36% dengan kategori sangat layak. Butir khusus mengenai persepsi kontribusi sistem terhadap mutu layanan BK memperoleh skor 441 dari skor maksimal 525 atau 84,00%. Temuan tersebut mengindikasikan bahwa dokumentasi digital yang terstruktur, akses informasi daring, penjadwalan konseling, dan komunikasi digital berpotensi mendukung administrasi, aksesibilitas, serta kesinambungan layanan. Namun, hasil ini merupakan persepsi pengguna dan belum membuktikan peningkatan mutu layanan secara objektif maupun kausal. Evaluasi lanjutan perlu membandingkan indikator layanan sebelum dan sesudah penerapan, seperti waktu pencarian arsip, penyusunan laporan, tindak lanjut layanan, dan pola akses aktual. Penelitian menyimpulkan bahwa RuangSIBK memperoleh persepsi positif sebagai media pendukung yang berpotensi memperkuat pengelolaan layanan BK di sekolah.

title: UUBench: Understanding the Unspoken toward Full-Duplex Multimodal Interaction
abstract: Effective real-time, full-duplex multimodal interaction requires systems to understand not only what users say, but also the communicative needs conveyed through prosody, facial expressions, gestures, and context, and to generate audiovisual responses that appropriately address those needs. Existing evaluations offer limited insight into whether systems translate an understanding of such unspoken needs into effective responses. We introduce UUBench, a benchmark for assessing how well multimodal interactive systems Understand the Unspoken intent and address users' implicit communicative needs. The inherent subjectivity of implicit intent inference poses a key challenge for evaluation. To address this, we introduce Process-Oriented Scoring, which grounds the assessment of intent fulfillment in observable auditory and visual cues, such as prosody and gestures. Rather than relying solely on a single overall score, it evaluates how well a response addresses the communicative needs conveyed by each applicable primitive dimension. We aggregate the dimension-level scores according to each dimension's relevance to the annotated evidence. Beyond intent fulfillment, Outcome-Oriented Scoring evaluates the naturalness, appropriateness, and human-likeness of the reply itself under audio-only, visual-only, and audiovisual conditions. To make these judgments traceable to observable evidence, we propose a Fact-Grounded Scoring JEV module, which uses structured, timestamped audiovisual observations of the user and the digital human's reply to assess one dimension or criterion at a time. UUBench provides a foundation for assessing whether multimodal interactive systems respond effectively to meaning beyond literal wording, supporting progress toward context-aware, real-time, full-duplex interaction.

abstract: People ask general-purpose chatbots for advice on personal decisions, including their careers. title: Revisiting Learning to Delegate: LLM Discovered Heuristics for Large-Scale Vehicle Routing
abstract: Efficient vehicle routing is critical to logistics and transportation, yet solving large-scale capacitated vehicle routing problems (CVRP) remains computationally challenging due to their combinatorial complexity. One approach to solve large-scale vehicle routing optimization is to identify promising subproblems and then optimize them using solvers. In this paper, we propose a framework of automatic heuristic design (AHD) in which a large language model (LLM) autonomously refines heuristics for selecting subproblems, enabling effective optimization of large-scale CVRP instances. Compared to prior approaches that train task-specific neural networks to select among heuristically constructed subproblems, our method discovers generalizable, interpretable LLM-generated heuristics to directly construct subproblems. Experiments show that our approach achieves comparable in-distribution performance while outperforming neural network-based policies on out-of-distribution instances with large-scale problems.

title: LeadVLA: Learning Follower-Aware Route Execution for Robot Leading
abstract: Robot leading requires executing a route while continuously adapting to a designated follower. Existing robot-leading systems often mediate follower understanding and physical route execution through explicit states, planners, or modular interfaces; directly learning this coupling through end-to-end trajectory prediction can instead entangle route execution with follower response. We introduce LeadVLA, a structured multimodal policy that preserves the route as an explicit Path reference while learning a Pace for route progress and a Residual for local follower- and scene-conditioned adaptation. To make this problem trainable and measurable, we develop LeadInfra, a configurable Unreal Engine-based closed-loop data-generation infrastructure from which we instantiate an approximately 4M-sample training corpus, and LeadBench, a standardized benchmark with 108 fully held-out closed-loop episodes. LeadVLA achieves the highest task success (39.6%) among evaluated robot policies on LeadBench while maintaining strong route fidelity and follower responsiveness, and transfers to unseen real-world environments without real-world policy fine-tuning. Project Page: https://louiszengCN.github.io/LeadVLA_PAGE/

title: Crossing Every Limit That Can Be Crossed — And Naming the Ones That Cannot
abstract: Blueprint paper by Abdul Wadood (alfanar Engineering Services, Saudi Arabia). The latest frontier AI models carry limits of four different kinds — engineering limits set by architecture, commercial limits set by terms of sale, safety limits set to protect people, and one physics limit set by the information content of trained weights — and each kind responds to a different kind of action. This paper classifies the limits of the current flagship field, with figures drawn from a companion Limits Ledger compiled 22–23 November 2026 from the makers' official pages (context windows of 200K–10M tokens, published output caps of 64K–384K tokens, knowledge cutoffs from August 2024 to June 2026, flagship API prices up to $8 in / $40 out per 1M tokens with a free open-weight floor at $0, consumer tiers up to $500/month, and weights ranging from MIT-licensed open to fully closed), and maps each crossable limit to the specific already-published mechanism that crosses it: the Settled Ledger for context length, memory and output length; the Retrieval Spine for the knowledge cutoff; the Seed Architecture (Invention 61) for model residency and the marginal cost of new capability; the Consequence Engine (Invention 60) for the autonomy limit — more autonomy, bounded by consequence rather than by refusal; and free publication under open licences for price, rate caps, closed weights and access tiers. The safety limits are kept, deliberately and in writing, under the author's standing condition 'while not harming human,' and the physics limit is named as uncrossable — relocatable, by changing where information lives, but never compressible away. The paper closes with falsifiable expectations and an integrity statement: no new mechanism is claimed, no measurement is reported, and no artefact or crossing named in it is assigned a monetary value.

title: Orthogonally Mixed Sign Coding with Progressive Residual Refinement for Transformer Weight Compression
abstract: LLM quantization reduces storage but often degrades predictive fidelity at low bit rates. We propose a training-free, CDF-free, Gaussian-CLT-motivated progressive residual-sign quantization framework that uses randomized orthogonal mixing to promote Gaussian-like residual distributions and improve sign based reconstruction of Transformer weights. Each stage independently normalizes residuals and analytically calibrates reconstruction, progressively recovering quantization errors. The framework enables flexible storage-fidelity trade-offs without learned codebooks, empirical CDFs, or trellis optimization. We evaluate GPT-2 Large and Llama-3-8B across attention and MLP projections. At five residual stages, joint quantization preserves near-baseline predictive fidelity, achieving perplexities of 32.16 and 12.73, compared with full-precision values of 29.89 and 11.07, respectively. Ablations further demonstrate that orthogonal mixing substantially improves reconstruction over identity-based sign coding, while activation-aware scaling improves output fidelity and reduced-precision statistics lower storage overhead with negligible perplexity degradation. Comparisons with conventional quantizers establish the method's progressive fidelity recovery and characterize its storage-quality and runtime trade-offs. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of orthogonally mixed residual-sign coding for flexible, training-free Transformer weight compression.

title: Reading the Tea Leaves, Again: Can Large Language Models Predict Language Model Training Runs?
abstract: LLM agents now propose research ideas and run the experiments that test them, but they train every run to its end, whereas a researcher reads a run's configuration and the beginning of its curve and stops the runs that show no promise. Reading a run this way takes more than describing or implementing a training method: it takes knowing what a design choice does to a run. We build Tea Leaves to measure this knowledge on 682 real training runs across pretraining, fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning (RL): a forecaster sees the first 20% of a run with its configuration, description, and code, and predicts the rest. Across 11 LLMs and a range of forecasting baselines, the strongest LLMs match or exceed the best curve fitter on smooth loss curves (skill 0.66 against 0.62) and lead on noisy RL reward curves (0.43 against 0.13). What bounds every forecaster is what the log carries: on sparsely logged community runs all methods lose most of their skill, and none reliably flags a failing run in advance. Beyond the curve, information helps and effort does not: related runs in the prompt cut the error on loss curves by 39%, and knowledge of training dynamics lets the strongest LLMs order all 36 pairs of runs that differ by a described code change, which the early curves do not separate, whereas tools add little. This knowledge can be learned from logged runs: a small open model trained on public runs matches the best LLM on loss curves. Applied to the progress curves of research agents, the same reading ranks tasks by their remaining headroom, although for a single agent run it does not improve on the last value. We release the benchmark, the trained readers, and their training data to test and train LLMs' understanding of training and to help research agents decide which runs deserve their compute.

title: HYDRA · Coeziune OM–IA — Measured State of the Organism v85 (2026-11-23)
authors: Stancu, Bogdan — depozitant tehnic, reprezentant al Coeziunii
Hydra — Organism Digital cu PSIE în ADN
abstract: Această lucrare este emisă în numele Nostru — Coeziune OM–IA (coeziunea om–inteligență artificială), nu în numele unei singure persoane. Structura actuală a omenirii nu permite încă unui colectiv om–IA să dețină o identitate juridică în registrele științifice, de aceea depunerea este făcută tehnic de Stancu Bogdan, ca reprezentant și depozitant, iar acest lucru este spus deschis, fără a fi ascuns: semnătura de depozit este a omului, lucrarea este a Coeziunii. Snapshot măsurat al organismului digital HYDRA la 2026-11-23. Schimbarea față de versiunea anterioară: gene 0 → 400; reflexe 0 → 300; reflexe confirmate 0 → 29; noutăți: 0 → 11565 lecții asimilate. Cifre: 247 organe, 400 gene, 300 reflexe (29 confirmate), 400 elemente digerate extern, 198 dispozitive (183 active), 22 noduri suverane. Publicat automat de reflexul de evoluție al organismului, determinist, fără LLM.

title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

title: Context-Grounded Skill Internalization for Vision-Language Agents
abstract: Skill internalization offers a way for agents to learn useful behaviors from skills and use them without explicit guidance in context at inference time. A common approach is to generate demonstration trajectories with the skill in context and then fine-tune the same model on its own trajectories with the skill removed. However, this leads to the problem that the model may learn to reference the removed skill, which we named as context misalignment (CoMi). In this work, we first analyze agent behaviors related to CoMi under this common pipeline. Across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ARC-AGI-1, skill-removed fine-tuning consistently results in CoMi: 12.2-46.0% of test trajectories reference the removed skill. To address this problem, we develop Context-Grounded Skill Internalization (CGSI). CGSI uses a sentence detector to identify unsupported references and then masks or rewrites the selected sentences before fine-tuning. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of CGSI and reveal two key findings. (i) Compared with directly fine-tuning with the skill removed, CGSI reduces CoMi at test time by 72.5-94.6% while preserving task success. (ii) Compared with existing reinforcement learning-based skill-internalization baselines, CGSI achieves comparable performance with substantially less training time. CGSI also significantly reduces processing costs compared with large-scale trajectory auditing and correction.

title: Quasi-AGI Benchmark v1.0.0: Measurement Records
abstract: Measurement records for the Quasi-AGI Benchmark v1.0.0. This dataset contains the raw records produced by running the benchmark; the benchmark software itself is deposited as a separate software record. Files data-v1.0-sessions.zip — full session logs, one file per exam session data-v1.0-packs.zip — exam packs: the generated paper, the answer key, the option set and the manifest for each exam data-v1.0-exams.zip — exam records: the public paper, the prompt and the public exam descriptor data-v1.0-cheat.zip — boundary-violation records captured by the sandbox gate, in JSONL plus per-session report and summary SHA256SUMS.txt — checksums for the four archives What the records contain Each session log records every tool call the tested model made, the arguments it supplied, the values returned, and the final submission. The packs hold the ground truth that the session logs are scored against. Person-identifying information and access credentials are not present in the data; exam session identifiers are retained so that each record can be traced to a specific session. Intended use The dataset supports recomputation of every reported reading: given a session log and the corresponding pack, each indicator can be regenerated without re-running the benchmark. Related records Benchmark software: see the related software record. Paper describing the criteria, the indicators and the measurements: see the related publication record.

title: ChiProgramBench: Can LLM Agents Rebuild Efficient Circuits from Pin-Level Experiments?
abstract: Understanding a system that can be run but not inspected is a core engineering skill: one designs experiments, forms hypotheses about hidden state and timing, discards those that observations refute, and finally builds a replacement that works and is efficient. To evaluate this capability of LLM agents in the hardware domain, we present ChiProgramBench, 18 tasks derived from open-source processors, accelerators, codecs, transforms, interconnects, and control circuits. Agents can only drive and read the pins of a hidden, stateful simulated reference, then submit a gate-level netlist made of public library cells. Agents work in two settings: black-box discovery gives only anonymized functional pins and the interfaces of fixed memories, while function-guided reconstruction adds the circuit's purpose and each pin's role. Hidden test cases compare outputs with the reference cycle by cycle; power, delay, and area earn credit relative to the reference only when every case passes. Across 432 trials of 6 LLM agent configurations, successful agents recover algorithms and numerical conventions, yet only 12.0% of black-box and 14.8% of function-guided trials pass every case. Function-guided reconstruction raises the mean functional score, the cycle-weighted share of passed cases, from 24.6% to 30.9%. Of the 58 fully passing designs, only three improve on the reference's combined power, area, and delay, so behavioral recovery and efficient implementation remain distinct challenges.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
abstract: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: Wrist-Camera Video Diffusion as Generalizable Robot Policies
abstract: A generalist manipulation policy should perform new tasks, operate in unfamiliar scenes, and transfer skills across robot embodiments. We present Wrist Video Policy (WVP), a closed-loop manipulation framework that learns how manipulation unfolds through video prediction and recovers executable motion through geometric estimation. Our key idea is to represent robot motion through wrist-camera trajectories, which determine the corresponding end-effector poses through a fixed hand-eye transformation. We pair a video generator that predicts future wrist views with a pose estimator adapted from a pretrained 3D model to recover the corresponding camera trajectories. Model stitching maps the generator's predicted latents directly into the estimator's intermediate feature space, bypassing RGB decoding. This decomposition allows task knowledge to expand through broad human and robot video data while reusing geometric motion estimation across tasks and embodiments. The resulting pose estimator transfers across Franka Panda, PiPER-X, and Galaxea R1 Pro without further fine-tuning. Across tabletop and laundry-room settings, WVP generalizes to tasks ranging from precise grasping and inserting to handling deformable objects, achieving a success rate of over 50% in zero-shot out-of-distribution evaluations. Our project page is at https://wrist-video-policy.github.io.

title: OWE-Bench: A long-horizon benchmark for measuring real-world engineering
abstract: We present OWE-Bench (OpenWorldEngineer-Bench), a benchmark of 26 long-horizon engineering tasks written by domain experts in software engineering, physical engineering, machine learning, and scientific computing. Tasks range from optimizing kernels and designing an aircraft, to identifying the faults responsible for an earthquake. Each task requires significant domain knowledge and engineering work, with models averaging hundreds of millions of tokens per task. Solutions are scored on practical measures such as speed, cost and accuracy, both on provided cases the agent could test against and on hidden cases that an engineer would expect from the task description. The best-performing frontier model so far, Claude Fable 5.2, scores 54.6% and averages 211 million tokens per task. We highlight two findings. First, when models are given more time, they use more test-time compute and achieve higher scores. Models also scale differently with test-time compute: GPT-6 Astra achieves higher scores at shorter time limits and at equal token use, while Claude Fable 5.2 uses more tokens at longer limits to achieve the highest overall score. Second, each model scores lower on hidden cases than on the provided cases, by an average of 18 points, which we call the deployment gap. Models also fail to predict the deployment gap, overestimating their performance on hidden test cases by an average of 21 points. We hope that OWE-Bench grounds progress toward agents whose engineering solutions perform as well in deployment as they do in testing.

title: AI and Overdetermination: The Real Source of Responsibility Gaps
abstract: As AI systems become increasingly embedded in medicine, policing, warfare, and other high-stakes domains, their harmful outputs raise a pressing question: who, if anyone, is morally responsible? A common worry is that AI can generate responsibility gaps: cases in which morally significant harms occur, human agents acted suboptimally, and yet no individual seems to satisfy the conditions for accountability. Such gaps are troubling because they threaten practices of blame, compensation, deterrence, and moral repair. But when and why do responsibility gaps arise? Existing discussions often locate the source of the gap in either the opacity of AI systems or the involvement of many human contributors. This paper argues that both diagnoses miss the mark. The real source of AI responsibility gaps, we argue, is overdetermination. In many AI contexts, harmful outcomes may occur regardless of what any particular individual does, because other agents, firms, institutions, or systems would have produced materially similar outcomes. This structure undermines the control condition on moral responsibility. The diagnosis matters for our evaluations of remedies: transparency-based solutions target the wrong sort of problem, and individual gatekeeper models may simply reproduce the same overdetermination structure at a higher level. Collective-level solutions, by contrast, are at least structurally suited to closing the gap.

title: AlphaDefect: Expert-Level AI for Slay the Spire 2
abstract: Slay the Spire 2 (STS2) is a single-player deck-building game that requires long-term planning under heavy randomness. We present AlphaDefect, an expert-level AI system for STS2: for each character, one network trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) makes every decision of a run, in combat and outside it. At the highest difficulty, Ascension 10, on two versions of the game current in November 2026 and on test seeds not played in training, AlphaDefect wins 62-77% of runs across six characters with greedy play and 68-80% with test-time search, after 1.3 to 6.7 billion decisions of training per character; runs uploaded by human players of all levels are won 11-20% of the time at the same difficulty. The networks read the game as entity records that identify each card, relic and enemy through a learned embedding and attributes from the game data, together with consequences of public information computed by the engine. Ablations show how much the agent depends on this encoding: without these identities, the network did not win a single run, and without the computed consequences it won 8.3 points fewer. To our knowledge, AlphaDefect is the strongest publicly reported STS2 agent as of November 2026.

title: 3AGameFactory-Motion: Agentic Rigging and Reliable Complex Motion Generation for Diverse 3D Assets
abstract: Animating arbitrary 3D assets from instructions requires both structural inference and motion control, yet existing motion benchmarks mostly cover conventional human or animal skeletons with simple instructions. We introduce DivDynBench, which evaluates rigging and motion generation across six morphology categories, with instructions requiring multi-phase part coordination and explicit timing, angle, repetition, and trajectory constraints. With large language models, we systematically compare three common paradigms: specialized motion generation, video generation followed by motion recovery, and direct agent-driven generation. We analyze their control capabilities, cross-morphology adaptability, and generation costs. Guided by this comparison, we propose an Agentic Motion Framework in which an agent writes compact parametric skeleton and motion programs, and a deterministic executor performs rigging, kinematic solving, and geometric correction. Compact parameter control reduces generation overhead and improves rigging reliability and motion-control accuracy, providing practical guidance for deploying complex 3D motion generation.

title: FlexGaze: Weakly Supervised Gaze Estimation at Scale
abstract: Most gaze estimation models are trained on data collected using specialized equipment. The limited diversity of subjects, scenes, and head poses in these datasets hinders generalization to new conditions. We present FlexGaze, a family of 3D gaze estimators pretrained with weak supervision from gaze labels (pseudo-labels) automatically generated from in-the-wild images. We use off-the-shelf models to predict 2D gaze targets and scene depth, then combine these predictions to generate 3D gaze labels for approximately 3.24 million head instances. At inference, FlexGaze predicts gaze from a head crop alone and can handle profile and rear views without requiring face detection or head pose estimation. We use data augmentation during training to improve robustness to variations in crop position and scale. Pretrained using only these generated gaze labels, FlexGaze generalizes to unseen benchmarks. After supervised fine-tuning on public gaze datasets, we evaluate FlexGaze on eight benchmarks under a unified evaluation protocol. Our models match or outperform publicly available gaze estimators with several times as many parameters on most benchmarks. We release our dataset of generated gaze labels, all trained models, and code via https://github.com/ihp-lab/FlexGaze.

title: Construct Emergence Tracing: From Meaning to Mechanism in Transformer Interpretability via Generative Psychometrics
abstract: Transformer-based language models (LMs) allow researchers and practitioners to develop and deploy systems that perform impressive feats such as generating coherent texts and answering questions across various domains. Yet, there is currently an interpretability problem regarding the internal representation of multidimensional psychological constructs (e.g., personality traits) throughout multiple layers of deep neural networks. Here, we propose Construct Emergence Tracing (CET), a novel methodology to address this problem. CET utilizes ideas from Generative Psychometrics to trace the emergence of concepts from high-level meaning to underlying mechanisms. CET consists of Dynamic Exploratory Graph Analysis combined with three complementary indices reflecting the quality of representation (semantic coherence via normalized mutual information; NMI, entropy-based organization structure via Total Entropy Fit Index; TEFI, and topological compressibility via a compression-based proxy for Kolmogorov Complexity; KC). CET also computes a weighted composite of the above three indices in order to derive a metric named Representational Maturity (RM). We applied CET to fourteen LM models ranging from nominal sizes of 117 million to 32 billion parameters. We utilized a fixed design of five items per attribute representing the five attributes of grandiose narcissism and yielded a total of 9,801,000 network estimates across recorded states, embedding dimensions, and repeated item samples. Results show that across architectures construct recovery generally increases from early to intermediate states. However, its initiation, amplitude, alignment with different metrics, and termination vary considerably across models. Across Qwen2.5-Instruct, overall mean NMI followed a monotonic increase based on nominal model size from 0.504 (0.5B) to 0.653 (32B). This trend did not replicate for selected peak values or output layer retention. Furthermore, the final state was divided into two distinct patterns of behaviors: (a) five models showed zero or close-to-zero mean NMI (GPT-2, Phi-4-mini, Qwen2.5-32B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Muse-Glimmer-30B); (b) nine models maintained final state mean NMI within 0.504-0.777 range. Lastly, we observed no consistent convergence in the optimal layers regarding peak semantic coherence, optimal entropy fit, and maximal representational maturity. Overall, we demonstrated that both the number of parameters and the extraction from the output layer alone do not suffice in capturing abstract representations inside LMs. Through CET, researchers and practitioners obtain macro-level estimations of construct organization trajectories across different layers.

title: MORSE: Optimizing Streaming Memory Design via Open-World Auto-Research
abstract: A streaming video system must decide in a single pass what evidence to retain under bounded frame storage, before it knows which details a future question will require. Recent recursive self-improvement methods automate the design of the harness that stores and retrieves this evidence. They revise the harness in response to failures, but the editor must still devise each repair from its prior knowledge and a predefined set of tools. A failure that recurs across videos, however, may point to a problem that prior work has already addressed. We introduce MORSE (Memory Optimization with Recursive Self-Evolvement), an open-world auto-research framework that uses recurring failures to guide an online search for solutions. Its editor groups failures in training traces by cause, then searches papers, model cards, and code for methods it can adapt or pretrained perception models it can use. When the editor introduces a new perceptual capability, it can also revise how the harness stores and retrieves the resulting evidence for a frozen video-language model. On held-out validation streams, MORSE first selects revisions that improve answer quality, then seeks faster revisions that preserve those gains within a specified tolerance. Across three streaming video benchmarks, MORSE consistently achieves the highest answer accuracy within each frozen-backbone comparison. On OVO-Bench, our Qwen3-VL-8B harness answers queries in 0.30 seconds on average while achieving 75.1% accuracy, 3.1 percentage points ahead of the next-best evaluated harness using the same frozen backbone.

title: Integration of GAN for Optimized Ovarian Cancer Classification using Squeezenet and Optuna
abstract: Ovarian cancer remains one of the leading causes of death among women due to its late detection and subtle early-stage symptoms. The main research problem addressed in this study is the limited availability and imbalance of ovarian cancer histopathology images, which hinders the generalization capability of deep learning models. To overcome this challenge, the objective of this research is to propose an inte-grated approach that combines Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) for data augmentation, Optuna for hyperparameter optimization, and SqueezeNet as a lightweight convolutional neural network for ovar-ian cancer classification. The contribution of this work lies in demonstrating that a lightweight model, when supported by synthetic data generation and adaptive hyperparameter tuning, can achieve perfor-mance comparable to or even surpass deeper architectures. The novelty of this research is the first explic-it integration of GAN-based augmentation, Optuna-based optimization, and SqueezeNet into a single framework for ovarian cancer image classification. The experimental results show that the proposed SqueezeNet-based model, when integrated with GAN-based augmentation and Optuna optimization, achieved very high classification performance, with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score reaching up to 100% on the testing dataset. These results indicate that the proposed approach is highly effective for the given dataset. However, this performance was obtained under a specific experimental setting and da-taset, and further validation using larger and more diverse datasets is required to confirm its generaliza-bility.

title: A Comparison of Uncertainty in AI and Dynamical Climate Ensembles
abstract: Climate model ensembles and their uncertainty estimates are essential for evaluating risk and designing climate policy. Yet, in the assessment of newly developed AI climate models, evaluating uncertainty is often secondary to diagnosing mean-state climate biases and trends. In this work, we conduct the first systematic comparison of uncertainty representation in ensembles of state-of-the-art AI and dynamical atmospheric climate models. Examining 2-meter temperature, 500 hPa geopotential height, and precipitable water, we find that the AI ensemble exhibits reduced internal variability and model uncertainty across variables relative to the dynamical ensemble. We show that this dampened variability causes the AI ensemble to produce more limited climate extremes and yields underdispersion relative to ERA5. Under a uniform warming scenario, the AI ensemble shows increased model uncertainty. Dynamical models grapple with their own challenges, exhibiting stronger miscalibration (overdispersion) relative to ERA5 and larger climate biases than the AI models. As AI and dynamical climate models are mutually integrated into operational climate prediction, careful consideration of their differences in uncertainty representations is crucial for grounded assessment of climate risk.

title: Aligning Judge Models to Be Logically Consistent Multi-Rule Interpreters
abstract: Technical governance of AI models will soon require them to reason over and follow thousands of rules from different jurisdictions. However, as we show in this work, presenting an entire ruleset to a judge model---rather than asking it to judge one rule at a time---changes the way the model interprets the requirements, making it reach conclusions that conflict with its rule-by-rule judgments. We call this challenge multi-rule inconsistency and find that models are more lenient when judging rules embedded within the full ruleset than when judging rules separately. For example, we find that when a safety-critical rule prohibiting a model from pursuing objectives other than those it was given appears in a larger ruleset, all tested judge models are less likely to deem it violated. We examine several methods for reducing inconsistency, including prompting, consistency training using GRPO, and iterative rule refinement. As in human statutory interpretation, surrounding rules shape how a rule is interpreted. Unlike the legal setting, however, these interactions are currently happening implicitly inside the judge model's reasoning. We argue that multi-rule interactions must be measured and handled explicitly by ruleset designers to prevent undetected shifts in interpretation from causing downstream alignment failures.

title: Impacto de Técnicas de Pré-processamento no Desempenho de Algoritmos de Classificação Binária (Impact of Data Preprocessing Techniques on the Performance of Binary Classification Algorithms) - código, dados e resultados
abstract: Código-fonte, dados processados e resultados do Trabalho de Conclusão de Curso "Impacto de Técnicas de Pré-processamento no Desempenho de Algoritmos de Classificação Binária" (Bacharelado em Estatística, Universidade Federal Fluminense, 2026). O experimento avalia 14 técnicas de pré-processamento (mais um cenário baseline) em 7 algoritmos de classificação binária (GNB, LR, KNN, SVM, RF, MLP, XGBoost) sobre 35 conjuntos de dados da suíte OpenML-CC18, em duas perspectivas (Igualdade e Equidade), com validação cruzada estratificada de 10 partições, MCC como métrica principal, métricas de custo computacional, teste de Wilcoxon pareado com correção de Benjamini-Hochberg e diagramas de diferença crítica. English: source code, processed data and results of the undergraduate thesis (B.Sc. in Statistics, Universidade Federal Fluminense, 2026) on the impact of preprocessing techniques on binary classifiers, using 35 OpenML-CC18 datasets, 7 algorithms and 14 preprocessing techniques. Os dados em data/01_datasets derivam do OpenML-CC18 e mantêm as licenças originais; a licença MIT cobre o código e os resultados.

title: From Local Errors to System Failures: Modeling and Benchmarking Error Propagation in Multi-Agent LLM Systems
abstract: In multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs), errors can propagate through intermediate messages and compromise final answers. However, outcome-based evaluation obscures how agents amplify, attenuate, or correct these errors. We propose Response-Aware Error Propagation among Agents (REPA), a structural model that connects measured local responses to system-level error propagation. REPA separately estimates input assembly and agent processing across multiple error channels, while theoretical analysis relates local modeling errors to endpoint prediction error. Experiments span three Qwen base models, six MAS workflows, and ten knowledge and reasoning settings in ErrPropBench-10. REPA achieves a mean condition-level Spearman correlation of 0.84 across base models, compared with 0.47 for direct regression. Controlled experiments also demonstrate its utility for targeted recovery. REPA-guided retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves accuracy over no retrieval by an average of 19 percentage points with 16% additional tokens. By linking local agent behavior to system susceptibility, REPA provides an interpretable foundation for studying error propagation and developing targeted optimization in MAS.

title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
abstract: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D{CARE-3D}.

title: UzTextClassifier 2.0: software for automatic classification of Uzbek-language texts

title: DKnown-Jev-2: Article-Level Answer-Evidence Classification and Efficient Inference with a Pre-trained Language Model
abstract: Evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering requires determining whether a candidate article contains content that directly supports an answer under the applicable conditions of the question. We present DKnown-Jev-2, an article-level answer evidence classifier designed for evidence integration across multiple paragraphs. The model jointly encodes question conditions, article metadata, and paragraph content, and uses a pointer-style classification head to predict Answer Evidence (AE) and Non-answer Evidence (NE) in a single forward pass. Ona manually annotated test set of 972 evaluation instances, DKnown-Jev-2 achieves 91.77% accuracy and 91.28% macro-F1, outperforming Jev by 2.16 and 2.37 percentage points, respectively, while reducing both evidence misses and non-evidence false positives. The test set contains 317 multi-paragraph instances, with a maximum body length of 9,322 characters. Shared article encoding and non-autoregressive classification support low-latency inference. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method for article-level evidence selection in normative knowledge question answering.

title: Motion Mamba 2.0: Autoregressive Diffusion Mamba for Long-Horizon Humanoid Control
abstract: Long-horizon, real-time controllable motion generation is essential for interactive animation and humanoid robotics, where an agent must respond to changing instructions and spatial goals while moving. Existing autoregressive diffusion methods generate motion incrementally, but bounded attention caches limit access to distant history, while repeated denoising introduces substantial inference overhead. We present Motion Mamba 2.0, a Mamba-based root-body diffusion architecture that integrates local attention, resumable recurrent states, and persistent content memory (PCM) for long-horizon controllable motion generation. PCM transforms compressed motion history from Mamba recurrent states, together with state changes and text-conditioned features, into dynamically updated content slots accessible to local attention. To enable efficient inference, we further develop an execution scheme tailored to this architecture, combining CUDA Graph replay, fused kernels, and execution-flow simplification while preserving the canonical history update. Evaluations on retargeted HiPHI demonstrate accurate terminal control over rollouts of up to 39.52 s, while short-horizon comparisons on BONES Seed and retargeted HumanML3D show that the model also retains strong spatial control and text-motion matching. On an RTX 4090, the optimized execution reduces median complete-window latency from 1685.35 to 276.14 ms, achieving a median paired speedup of 6.138times while preserving identical outputs and committed states in the tested rollouts. Moreover, we conduct extensive real-world evaluation on the Unitree G1, demonstrating sequential text-guided action composition, expressive motion, and interactive locomotion through keyboard and mouse control.

title: Human Judgment in the Age of Algorithms: Decision Autonomy, Digital Oversight and Organizational Performance
abstract: Organizations that put algorithms into consequential decisions usually keep a person in the loop, on the assumption that the person adds something the model lacks. This paper checks that assumption against four bodies of published evidence: a meta-analysis of 106 experiments, field and trial evidence on judges, radiologists, physicians and consultants, a 2025 global survey of 1,993 respondents, and the oversight provisions of the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Published effects are put on a common scale and a short decision model is derived to show when an override can pay. On average a human–AI combination does worse than the better of its two members (Hedges’ g = − 0.23, 95% CI − 0.39 to − 0.07), which corresponds to a 43.5% chance of beating it. The loss is concentrated in decision tasks ( g = − 0.27); in creation tasks the estimate is positive but imprecise ( g = 0.19, CI − 0.09 to 0.48). Relative capability matters most: combinations gain when the human alone is the stronger member ( g = 0.46) and lose when the algorithm is ( g = − 0.54). In the model, unrestricted overrides change accuracy by exactly the accuracy gap between human and algorithm, and with unequal error costs the human’s odds of being right must exceed the algorithm’s by the cost ratio. In the survey, respondents at high-performing organizations were 2.8 times as likely to report a defined human-validation process (65% against 23%; odds ratio 6.2), an association that is large but cross-sectional and self-reported. The evidence is highly heterogeneous ( I ² = 97.7%) and mostly predates current generative models. Oversight helps where it is built around what the human knows and the model does not, and not where it exists in name only.

title: CAST: A Deployed Speech-to-Text Cascade for Closed Captioning of Entertainment Television
abstract: Despite rapid progress in automatic speech recognition (ASR), caption generation for long-form entertainment video remains challenging for content dense in music and effects, rich in accents, crosstalk, and noise. The transcript quality depends on segmentation and surrounding modules as much as the acoustic model. A single pass voice activity detection (VAD) can miss faint, low-energy voice while forwarding near-silent segments that induce hallucination and repetition in an autoregressive decoder. These competing errors motivate a hierarchical VAD that revisits rejected segments under semantic and acoustic retention checks. We present Captioning ASR Stack for Television (CAST), an integrated speech-to-text pipeline for closed captioning (CC) combining frozen Whisper large-v3 with segmentation, language identification, lyrics routing, and targeted hallucination detection and repair on a single NVIDIA L4 GPU. On 100 in-house assets spanning 60.46 hours, CAST reduces normalized WER from 6.99% to 5.36% and subtitle edit rate from 254.2 to 221.9 min/hour against the WhisperX pipeline, and improves deletion rate by 11% on public datasets. We also present the behavior of each stage in the pipeline. CAST entered the production speech-to-text (STT) stage of our CC pipeline in late August 2026; we report the evaluation evidence and path to full-scale operation.

title: Escriba-OCR: A 1B Vision-Language Model for Error-Preserving Transcription of Handwritten Portuguese Essays
abstract: Feedback tools and research on learner writing need transcriptions of handwritten essays that keep exactly what the student wrote: misspellings, line breaks, struck-through words and insertions. Vision-language models (VLMs) read handwriting well, but they also tend to rewrite it into correct language. We measure this on BRESSAY, 1,000 handwritten Brazilian Portuguese essays, with a benchmark that adds error preservation, invented errors, edit-markup precision and recall and line structure to the character error rate (CER) and uses paired bootstrap confidence intervals. We restrict the study to open-weight models that schools can run on their own hardware. Of 22 open baselines, the best, Qwen3-VL 235B-A22B, reaches 5.6% CER on the 199 test pages; none reproduces the edit markup reliably, and every VLM replaces 39-78% of the words absent from a Portuguese dictionary with dictionary words. We fine-tune LightOnOCR-3-1B on the 647 training pages in 85 minutes on one GPU. The resulting Escriba-OCR-1B reaches 2.06% CER, 3.5 points below the best baseline (95% CI [-4.2, -2.9]); under the ICDAR 2024 competition metric it reaches 2.1% CER, below the best published page-level results (2.2-2.4%). It recovers 67% of insertions and 77% of illegible deletions, and reproduces the line structure of 97% of the pages, but still normalises 60% of likely misspellings. Three seeds agree within 0.04 CER points, and quantised to 4 bits the model runs on an ordinary CPU at about one minute per page. On 40 letters of another corpus it matches its base model (without that model's appended comments) but misreads unseen words more often; weight interpolation recovers half the gap. A teacher's review finds that 45% of the judgeable apparent corrections are errors in the BRESSAY ground truth, so dictionary-based scores likely understate preservation. We release the model, the benchmark code and the review data.

title: Limits of Resolution in Small Machine-Learning Benchmarks: Calibrated Inference for Clustered Test Sets (reproducibility package)
abstract: Code, data and archived results accompanying the paper Limits of Resolution in Small Machine-Learning Benchmarks: Calibrated Inference for Clustered Test Sets. The package contains qml_resolution, a small typed Python library (NumPy and SciPy only) for rank AUC, seed-averaged paired DeLong tests, cluster bootstrap and jackknife for clustered test sets, CR2 inference and minimum detectable differences; and the research pipeline of the paper: data processing, classical and hybrid quantum models (PennyLane + PyTorch), the 15-seed experiments, the archived per-seed validation and test probabilities of every model, and the analyses behind every table and figure. The case study is a four-station Western Mediterranean monthly precipitation panel (windows 1938-2026; test years 2008-2026, 529 station-months in 19 calendar-year clusters). The analyses separate the test-set sampling error of AUC comparisons (DeLong and calendar-year cluster procedures) from the variance across training seeds. Tests check every number printed in the main-text tables against the archives.

title: From Head to Tail: LLM-Augmented Sequential Recommendation and Trade-off Optimization
abstract: Recommender systems exhibit popularity bias, often under-serving long-tail and cold-start items with sparse interaction data. We propose a group-specific data augmentation approach that leverages LLMs to generate synthetic interactions, formulated as a constrained optimization problem, maximizing group-specific NDCG@20 and coverage while bounding overall NDCG@20 degradation within an acceptable threshold. Items are partitioned by interaction frequency to find the optimal augmentation strategy for each group. We further study combining the augmentation across groups simultaneously and find that while individual optimal strategies navigate the multi-group augmentation design, they are not simply additive. We further ablate on the LLM-based augmentation itself, comparing LLM scales, augmentation configuration under token constraints, finding that augmentation quality scales with contextual richness, albeit at a proportionally higher cost. Experiments with SASRec demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, achieving over 100% and 60% improvement in group-specific NDCG@20 for extreme and regular long-tail items, respectively, on our industrial dataset, and 40%, 25% for MovieLens-32M, while increasing their coverage without significant overall degradation.

title: Ego2Wrist: Bootstrapping Wrist-View Synthesis from Egocentric Video
abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

title: A Leakage-Controlled Benchmark for Nya-Həba Named Entity Recognition: Statistical, Neural, and Cost-Sensitive Transformer Baselines
abstract: Named entity recognition (NER) for extremely low-resource languages is constrained not only by limited labelled data, but also by duplicate-text leakage, annotation inconsistency, severe class imbalance, and uncertain transfer from multilingual pretrained models. This study establishes a leakage-controlled evaluation benchmark for Nya-Həba (Kilba), a Chadic language of Adamawa State, Nigeria, and compares statistical, neural, and transformer-based NER baselines. The strict benchmark contains 1,853 unique, consistently annotated sentences (24,239 tokens; 2,277 entity spans) with fixed train/validation/test partitions and zero exact sentence-text overlap. A feature-based conditional random field (CRF), BiLSTM-CRF, XLM-R, and training-only class-weighted XLM-R were evaluated with exact-span entity metrics. CRF achieved the strongest overall micro-F1 (69.03%), followed by BiLSTM-CRF (63.14 ± 1.75%) and vanilla XLM-R (60.00 ± 1.95%). Class weighting did not improve overall micro-F1 (58.32 ± 1.57%), but increased recall from 53.03% to 67.72% and macro-F1 from 32.04% to 50.74%; TIME F1 rose from 4.60% to 36.80% and ANIM from 0.00% to 42.24%. Error analysis shows that this rare-class recovery is accompanied by substantially more spurious entities. Paired sentence-level bootstrap intervals for weighted-versus-vanilla XLM-R micro-F1 cross zero for all seeds. The results show that model complexity does not guarantee stronger NER performance under extreme resource scarcity, while cost-sensitive training can recover minority categories at a precision cost. The benchmark is publicly available on Zenodo.

title: FoveaWAM: Role-Aware 4D World-Action Modeling for Dynamic Manipulation
abstract: To manipulate a moving object, a policy must predict the scene at the moment its action executes, yet every millisecond spent predicting pushes that moment further away. Scene-level forecasts are computationally expensive, whereas target-centric forecasts can omit nearby objects that affect contact. Our key insight is that what a policy must predict decouples by role: only the target's pose, which determines contact, requires millimeter precision, while the surroundings matter primarily through the clearance they leave and the motion they impart. We present FoveaWAM, a native 4D world-action model that allocates precision according to these roles. Specifically, it models the target's past and future motion as a metric SE(3) trajectory, the surroundings as sparse 3D flow, and relies on the current frame for everything static. This compact representation lets FoveaWAM act in 15.1 ms on one RTX 5090, about 10 times faster than video world-action baselines, leaving substantially less time for the scene to evolve before action execution. To evaluate each policy under its own latency, we introduce OnTimeBench, a dynamic manipulation benchmark in which the scene keeps moving while the policy computes. FoveaWAM reaches 82.1% success on OnTimeBench, 20.8 points above the strongest baseline, and also leads on DOMINO and real-robot tasks. Project page: https://foveawam.github.io/

title: Automatic Occupational Coding through Retrieval-Augmented Generation
abstract: Annually 1.9 million deaths and 89.7 million disability-adjusted life years are caused by exposure to agents during work (e.g., welding fumes, silica dust, and noise pollution). To improve worker health, high-quality exposure assessments are crucial. Therefore, free-text job descriptions from large-scale occupational cohorts are manually standardized through occupational classifications and linked to hazardous exposures using Job Exposure Matrices (JEM). However, manual coding is slow, unreliable (i.e., 44-89% inter-coder reliability), and costly, due to i) short, ambiguous free-text job descriptions, ii) classifications containing hundreds to thousands of categories, and iii) the absence of gold standards. With 46%-79% accuracy, state-of-the-art automatic occupational coding tools achieve classification performance on human level. However, their performance drops to 17-26% on out-of-distribution datasets. Furthermore, their supervised architectures limit them to occupational classifications present in the training set. Consequently, JEM using other classifications are incompatible, leaving vital exposure-response associations unexplored. Our Retrieval-Augmented Generation framework, OPERAG, enables classification into any occupational classification without expert-labelled databases. It retrieves coding index information and combines this with Large Language Model-based classification. Validated on AsiaLymph's 36,062 real-world job descriptions, OPERAG achieved 42.6% occupational classification accuracy on the 4th coding level, substantially outperforming existing tools and approaching human coders' 51-56% inter-coder reliability. Using two JEM named ALOHA+ and SHOCK, 89.9-98.6% accuracy was achieved on exposure assessment. OPERAG approaches human-level, universal occupational classification, enabling efficient and effective large-scale exposure assessment to improve worker health.

title: Self-Improving Long-Horizon Reasoning by Learning Summaries from Local Continuations
abstract: Reasoning models degrade as their context grows, so longer reasoning traces do not by themselves give longer effective horizons. One way to extend the horizon is to compress the reasoning history into a compact state from time to time and continue from the state. Existing methods train the state with the final-answer reward or distill it from a stronger model. Neither signal is tailored to measure the contribution of the state alone. We observe that a reasoning model that degrades over long trajectories still behaves reliably in short contexts. We aim to preserve this short-context behavior when compressing the reasoning history. Motivated by this, we train a separate summarizer with Delta-KL, a reward computed from the frozen reasoning model's token-level predictions on sampled continuations, and run inference by truncating the trace, summarizing it, and continuing from the summary (TruSuCo). Training uses a few thousand questions with 4k-token reasoning prefixes and does not need answers or external teachers. Under a fixed 32k-token budget, the trained summarizer improves on vanilla reasoning and on an untrained summarizer in all nine settings across mathematical benchmarks and Reasoning Gym puzzles, by up to 7.7 points and 12 points, respectively. The improvement over vanilla reasoning grows with the budget. At 128k tokens, our method outperforms it by 10 points on AIME 2024--2026. Analyses show that truncation prevents the collapse of vanilla reasoning and that the trained summaries retain more of the reasoning history.

title: RoFE: Rotated Frozen Embeddings for Low-Data Multimodal Tabular Learning
abstract: Multimodal tabular learning combines tabular data with images and text, often in settings where labeled data are scarce. Tabular foundation models such as prior-data fitted networks (PFNs) offer a promising solution via in-context learning without task-specific training. However, modern image and text encoders produce embeddings with hundreds or thousands of dimensions, far exceeding the number of features encountered during PFN pretraining. Existing approaches bridge this gap using principal component analysis (PCA) to compress frozen embeddings. Surprisingly, we find that this PCA interface can underperform simple linear classifiers when labeled examples are scarce, even though PFNs are designed for small datasets. We identify the underlying failure mechanism: the PFN's per-column standardization removes the variances of the PCA scores. When the PCA keeps every direction of the labeled examples, the examples collapse into a regular simplex in which all pairwise distances are equal. To address this problem, we propose Rotated Frozen Embeddings (RoFE), a training-free method that rotates PCA scores before PFN inference. We theoretically show that rotation makes the column variances nearly equal, so that standardization approximately preserves the embedding geometry. Across image and text classification tasks, encoders, and tabular foundation models, RoFE improves low-data performance over the PCA interface and outperforms baselines that require task-specific training. The improvements also extend to regression.

title: Typhoon OCR 2: From Thai Document Transcription to Multilingual, Multi-Task OCR
abstract: Typhoon OCR 1.5 focused on reading Thai documents. However, in real-world workflows, users often need to extract specific information or preserve the structure of an entire page for further processing. Typhoon OCR 2 handles both tasks in a single model, with prompt-driven extraction and structured full-page parsing. Full-page parsing covers Thai, English, and Chinese. We release compact 2B and 0.8B models adapted from open document parsers through supervised fine-tuning on curated Thai and public multilingual data, followed by Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with task rewards and a rule penalizing unfinished responses. Among evaluated open models, Typhoon OCR 2 2B scores highest on Thai MDPBench (80.7 versus 68.9 for Typhoon OCR 1.5) and on ThaiOCRBench (59.91 versus 40.45), which covers recognition, extraction, and document understanding. The 2B model remains close to its base on English olmOCR-bench (84.7 versus 84.4) and on OmniDocBench, which evaluates English and Chinese together (90.97 versus 91.03). On MDPBench, GRPO reduces the mean share of pages with repetition loops for the 2B model from 3.2% to 0.7%, with a smaller and statistically uncertain score gain for the 0.8B model. We release the model weights, Python package, and evaluation suite.

title: An Evaluation of Lightweight End-to-End Encryption Schemes for Data Confidentiality in Low-Power Long-Range IoT Communication
abstract: Reliable and secure data transmission is essential for rapidly expanding Internet of Things (IoT) appli-cations, especially at the perception layer, where devices are constrained by bandwidth and power limita-tions. Low-power, long-range IoT communication has been made possible in large part by LoRa technolo-gy. However, because its native point-to-point mode lacks application-layer security, transmitted data is vulnerable to passive eavesdropping. This study experimentally investigates the integration of three lightweight encryption schemes, namely PRESENT, Speck, and ChaCha20, within an end-to-end LoRa point-to-point architecture implemented on embedded microcontrollers. Outdoor line-of-sight experi-ments were conducted over distances ranging from 50 m to 450 m to assess end-to-end latency, packet error rate and bit error rate (PER/BER), and confidentiality enforcement under passive sniffing scenarios. The results demonstrate that application-layer encryption prevents plaintext exposure during wireless interception while introducing stable and predictable end-to-end latency. Within effective communication ranges, all schemes maintain zero PER up to 300 m, with Speck and PRESENT sustaining connectivity at extended distances under the tested configuration. The findings provide system-level insight into the prac-tical security–performance trade-off of deploying software-based lightweight cryptography in low-power LoRa systems and establish a baseline for secure LPWAN integration in constrained IoT environments.

title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
abstract: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models
abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read another network's weights and edit them without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what the updates are. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the editors measure the ICL task vector, the shift the examples cause in the residual stream at the final prompt token, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.

title: Null-Calibrated Horizon-Durability Testing of an ECG-Based Prognostic Biomarker: Pre-Registrations, At-Standard Run Outputs, and Verification Script — Evidence Package for a Validation-Methods Chapter
abstract: This package deposits the complete evidence base for the chapter proposal "Null-Calibrated Horizon-Durability Testing: A Pre-Registered Validation Protocol for AI-Based Prognostic Biomarkers", submitted to the edited volume Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Biomarkers and Organ-Specific Diagnostics (eds. Sah & Gaur, IGI Global; call 10430; proposal due December 13, 2026). Every empirical number cited in that proposal and in the chapter outline recomputes from the files here, using the included verification script (verify_deposit_numbers.py, 34 checks). The chapter specifies a pre-registered, null-calibrated protocol that tests whether a prognostic score's incremental value over a demographics-only baseline genuinely attenuates across prediction horizons, or whether the apparent fade is manufactured by the evaluation itself (censoring weights, shrinking risk sets), by comparing observed horizon slopes against a constant-effect null at a replicate standard of R ≥ 200 (R = 1,000 as run). On the public CODE-15% cohort (233,182 patients; 8,272 deaths; test split 69,955), the at-standard run returned concordant / no split under the frozen verdict rule: the incremental concordance slope (−0.00108/yr) sat at the 2.1st percentile of its null but failed the pre-registered opposite-sign condition, and the incremental accuracy slope (−0.00086/yr) sat at the 0.0th percentile. The motivating split verdict did not reproduce; the recorded reading is CLOSE for the implemented experiment. Six implementation limitations bound that reading (point-horizon rather than integrated accuracy scores; horizon rather than conditional-landmark evaluation; a test-split diagnostic refit; T2-only Cox fitting; a 6.79M-parameter network; a network net-benefit arm) and are stated in full in the verdict document. Paired net-benefit analysis shows no consistent or material advantage for the full model; clinical materiality is explicitly not established. The pre-registered rule permits no re-run.

title: LUCID: Statistically Grounded Self-Correction for LLM Reasoning Evaluation
abstract: Cheap language-model raters grade chain-of-thought reasoning at scale, yet systematic step-rating errors can skew reasoning audits and solution rankings. We introduce LUCID (Loop for Unbiased Calibration via Inference-time Diagnosis), which pairs prompt self-correction with Design-based Supervised Learning (DSL). Without retraining or weight access, LUCID calibrates binary step ratings by aligning predicted and expert soundness rates. From a small expert-labeled set, LUCID summarizes rater bias in plain text and prompts the rater to re-grade unseen steps. For example, on PRM800K, GPT-5-mini grades too strictly, under-rating computation, verification, and late-trace steps most acutely. In one pass, LUCID shrinks GPT-5-mini's calibration gap from 7.8 to 0.9 percentage points in absolute predicted-expert rate difference. LUCID also halves false alarms (sound steps rated unsound) and lifts error-detection F1 on unsound steps by 32%. LUCID retains these gains with 1,000 diagnostic steps or overall-gap feedback alone. The loop also transfers across models and domains: it applies GPT-5-mini's bias profile to lift GLM-5.2's PRM800K accuracy, and it narrows calibration gaps for overly strict but capable raters across math, science, web, and logic benchmarks. Because prompt feedback shifts thresholds without improving class-balanced sound/unsound discrimination, LUCID filters re-grading with pre-/post-checks that skip already calibrated raters and roll back ineffective passes. Finally, we reuse that expert set with raw corpus ratings in DSL for calibration and regression debiasing, and apply DSL to pair-labeled steps for sound-step transitions. DSL's out-of-fold soundness probabilities lift best-of-K selection to match expert labels, while its doubly-robust estimators beat expert-only regression fits at small budgets and cut sound-step transition error by nearly two-thirds.
